en: At the head of the dawns, the great one has stood up erect; emerging from the darkness, he has come with light.
Agni, with his brilliant luster and beautiful limbs, having been born, has filled all the dwellings. Born as the offspring of heaven and earth, O Agni, you are lovely, distributed among the plants.
The brilliant infant has passed through the darkness and the nights; crying out loudly, he has gone forth from his mothers toward the cows.
Viṣṇu, knowing thus his highest [step], the great one born, has stepped upon the third. When they have offered him the milk of his own mouth, those who are of one mind worship him here.
From there, the mothers who bear the nourishment approach you with foods, for you are the increaser of food.
You go toward them again, assuming other forms; you are the Hotṛ-priest among the human clans.
[I invoke] the Hotṛ of the rite, whose chariot is brilliant, the shining banner of every sacrifice.
By his greatness, he stands as the counterpart of every god through his splendor—Agni, the guest of men.
Clothed in beautifully adorned garments, Agni, born at the navel of the earth, the ruddy one, has become the domestic priest; as king, he sacrifices to the gods here.

For you, O Agni, have always extended across both Heaven and Earth, as a son [stretches] over his two mothers. Come forth, O youngest one, to those who long for you; then, O powerful one, bring the gods here.
Satisfy the longing gods, O youngest one; knowing the seasons, O Lord of Seasons, sacrifice here.
O Agni, with those who are the divine officiants, you are among the hotṛ-priests the most skilled in sacrifice.
You perform the office of the *hotṛ* and the *potṛ* for the people; you are the wise thinker (*mandhātṛ*), the giver of wealth, and the observer of cosmic order (*ṛtāvā*).
With the cry of *svāhā*, let us prepare the oblations; may the god Agni, as the worthy one, worship the gods.
We have come to the path of the gods that we may follow it as far as we are able.
May Agni, the wise one, perform the sacrifice; he is the Hotṛ priest; may he arrange the rites and the seasons.

O gods, if we, being more ignorant, violate the vows of you who are wise— RV_10.002.03.1 {30} We have come to the path of the gods, that we may follow it as far as we are able. RV_10.002.03.2 {30} Agni, the knowing one, shall sacrifice; he is the Hotṛ; he shall ordain the rites and the seasons. RV_10.002.04.1 {30} Whatever vows of yours we, the less wise, violate, O gods who are more wise—
Agni, the wise one, shall fulfill all that with these seasons by which he ordains the gods.
When mortals, with simple minds and feeble resolve, do not attend to the sacrifice, Agni—
the Hotṛ who knows the sacred rites and is the most excellent sacrificer— shall discern it and worship the gods according to their seasons.
For the progenitor begot you as the bright banner and the face of all sacrifices. As such, win for us lands rich in heroes, desirable food, and wealth that benefits all people.
You, whom Heaven and Earth, whom the Waters, whom Tvaṣṭṛ, and whom the well-born one have brought forth.

Knowing well the path traveled by the fathers, O Agni, shine forth brilliantly as you are kindled. The lord, the king, the messenger, kindled and impetuous, has appeared for the sake of skillful power;
he shines forth with great light, driving away the dark night with his radiant glow.

When he, assuming a form, approached the dark one—the maiden born of the great father—he established the upward-shining light of the sun; as the messenger of heaven, he shines with his riches. Accompanied by the auspicious one, the auspicious one has arrived; the lover has come after his sister from behind.
RV 10.3.3: With well-marked days, Agni, spreading abroad, has overcome the dark with his radiant colors.
RV 10.3.4: His journeys, like those of the great roaring one, kindle the voices of the auspicious friend, Agni;
the bright, blazing rays of the worshipful, mighty bull have shone forth upon his path.
Whose radiant splendors flow like sounds, he who is shining, lofty, and of fair days;
he who reaches the sky with his most excellent, most brilliant, playful, and most exalted beams of light. His powers, whose fellies are visible, roar as he speeds along with his teams.
He, the most divine, the far-reaching messenger, shines with ancient, radiant, and resonant flames.
As the messenger of Heaven and Earth, the youthful pair, bring us great wealth and sit down among us.
May Agni, swift with his swift horses, impetuous with his impetuous steeds, come hither to us.
I sacrifice to you; I send forth this thought to you, so that you may become worthy of praise in our invocations.
O Agni, ancient King, you are like a watering-place in the desert for the man who desires to worship.
O most youthful one, to you the people come together as cattle seek a warm stall.
You are the messenger of the gods and of mortals; great within, you move through the radiant realm.
Like a noble infant, your mother, cherishing you, supports you as she seeks your company.
From the height you descend by a steep slope, longing for it; like a beast let loose, you strive to win the prize.
O wise one, we are foolish; O Agni, you alone truly know your own greatness.
The covering lies still, yet he moves, devouring with his tongue; as the lord of the people, he repeatedly licks the youthful maiden.
He is born ever anew in ancient woodlands; gray-haired and smoke-bannered, he has taken his stand in the forest.
Like a bull that has not bathed in water, he does not go forth—he whom mortals, being of one mind, bring together.

Like two thieves who have risked their lives, the two seekers of the forest have bound him with ten cords. This is a newer hymn for you, O Agni; yoke your chariot as it were with its bright-limbed parts.
O Jātavedas, may this prayer and this song of homage ever be for your increase.
O Agni, protect our children and our progeny; guard our bodies as well, never being heedless.
The one ocean, the support of riches, whose many births spring from us, gazes upon our hearts.
RV 10.5.1: He clings to the udder of the two breasts; the bird’s foot is placed in the midst of the spring.
RV 10.5.2: Dwelling in a common nest, the bulls have united with the mares;
the sages guard the station of *ṛta*; they have established secret names in the distance.
The two faithful and artful ones have united; having measured him out, they brought forth the infant and nurtured him.
Moving toward the navel of all that is firm and moving, they follow with their minds the mental thread of the Sage.
For the paths of Truth, from of old, accompany the well-born one, providing nourishment for his strength.
Wearing the upper garment of heaven and earth, they have grown strong with the clarified butter and the foods of honey.
Desiring the seven ruddy sisters, the wise one has brought forth the honey for all to behold.
Born of old, he has rested within the mid-air; seeking it, he found the covering of Pūṣan.
The poets have fashioned seven boundaries; across one of them the transgressor has gone. Indeed, the pillar stands in the abode of the highest Āyu, at the parting of the paths, upon the foundations.
Non-being and being are in the highest heaven, in the birthplace of Dakṣa, in the lap of Aditi.
Agni is indeed our first-born of *ṛta*, the bull at the earliest age, shining like a milch-cow.
This is he, under whose protection and through whose favors the singer prospers in Agni’s assistance;
he who, radiant and encompassed by the highest beams of the *ṛṣis*, moves all around.
Agni, who shines forth with his splendors, radiant with the gods, the observer of *ṛta*, the eternal;
he who has extended his friendship to his friends, unassailable like a swift steed;
he who rules over every feast for the gods, and rules over all life at the dawning of the morning.

Upon whom the mind rests as it offers oblations into Agni—he, whose chariot is unharmed, supports [the world] with his powers. Increasing through his powers and delighting in hymns, he hastens toward the gods with rapid flight. As the joyous invoker and the most skilled sacrificer, Agni, mingling with the gods, sprinkles them with his ladle.
Bring hither with songs and prostrations that Agni who trembles like Indra at the dawn;
him whom the sages praise with their hymns as Jātavedas, the one to be invoked by the victorious.
In whom all treasures have gathered together, as horses with their riders hasten toward the prize.
O Agni, bring hither to us those aids most desired by Indra and Vāta.
For indeed, O Agni, having sat down with greatness, as soon as you were born, you became worthy of oblations. The gods followed that intention of yours; then the first protectors increased in power.

O Agni, bestow upon us well-being from heaven and from earth for all our life’s duration, O God, so that we may perform sacrifice. May we be united with your insights, O Wonder-worker; protect us, O God, with your far-reaching blessings.
These hymns, O Agni, have been born for you; they celebrate your favor with gifts of cattle and horses.
When the mortal has attained enjoyment according to his portion, O Vasu, holding [the oblation] with his thoughts,
O well-born one— then I honor Agni as father, Agni as kinsman, Agni as brother, and always as a friend.
I worship the face of the great Agni, the bright and worshipful light of Sūrya in heaven.
O Agni, may our prayers be successful and winning, for you, the eternal Hotṛ, protect us within our home.
May he who is true to the cosmic order (*ṛta*), possessed of ruddy horses and abundant food, grant us desirable wealth through these days and nights.
Like a well-placed friend, may he be like a long-established ritual priest, the lover of the sacrifice, through the days.
With their two arms, the seekers have generated Agni; they have established him as the Hotṛ-priest among the people.
O God, sacrifice yourself to the gods in heaven! What can the ignorant and simple-minded man do for you?
Just as you have sacrificed to the gods according to the seasons, O God, so too sacrifice to yourself, O well-born one.
Be our protector and guardian, O Agni; be the maker of our strength and the giver of vigor to us.
Grant us, O most mighty one, the offering of oblations, and protect our bodies with unwearied care.
Agni advances with his lofty banner; like a bull, he bellows toward the two worlds.

He has reached even the furthest ends of heaven; like a buffalo, he has grown strong in the lap of the waters. The embryo, the bull with the hump, has rejoiced; the vigorous calf, never failing, has bellowed. Making the divine powers rise up, he goes forth as the first one among his own dwellings.
He who has seized the head of his parents; at the sacrifice, they have established him as the ocean of the sun.
At his flight, the ruddy ones, whose base is the horses, have delighted in their bodies within the womb of *ṛta*.
O Vasu, you indeed go at the forefront of every dawn; you have become the radiant one between the two twins.
For the sake of *ṛta*, you have established the seven steps, engendering Mitra for your own self.
You have become the eye and the great guardian of *ṛta*; you become Varuṇa when you go to the one who observes *ṛta*.
O Jātavedas, you have become the Son of the Waters; you have become the messenger for him whose oblation you enjoy.
You are the leader of the sacrifice and of the mid-world, where you accompany [the sacrificer] with your auspicious teams of horses.
You have established your head in heaven, O winner of light; you have made your tongue, O Agni, the bearer of the oblation.
Trita, by his mental power, chose him within the cave, seeking the prayer of the highest father according to his ways.
Being attended by his parents in their lap, calling his weapons kin, he goes forth.
Knowing the weapons of his fathers, the son of Aptya, impelled by Indra, went forth to battle.
Having slain the three-headed, seven-rayed one, Trita released the cows of Tvaṣṭṛ’s son.
RV 10.008.09.1: Indra, the lord of the virtuous, struck down with his might the one who was seeking to rise up excessively, thinking himself [invincible].
RV 10.008.09.2: Of Viśvarūpa, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, he shattered the three heads and carried off the cattle.
RV 10.009.01.1: O Waters, you indeed are sources of bliss; grant us strength for our nourishment.
For the great spectacle to behold— That most auspicious sap of yours, grant us a share of it here,
Like longing mothers for their children.
Let us go gladly to you, for whose abode you quicken us; O Waters, give us life.
May the divine Waters be auspicious for our aid and for our drink.
May they flow toward us for our well-being and prosperity.
I implore the goddesses who rule over desirable things and govern the people,
for their healing medicine.
Soma has told me within the waters that all healing remedies are there, as well as Agni, who brings well-being to all.
O Waters, bestow healing remedies as a protection for my body.
May we long behold the sun. O Waters, carry away whatever sin is in me—
whatever I have committed as treachery, or whatever curse or falsehood I have uttered.
I have followed after the waters today; we have united with their essence.
O Agni, come hither full of milk; endow me with splendor.
Even as a friend, I would turn a friend toward me, having traveled across even the vast ocean.
May the wise one, contemplating the future, establish the grandson of the father upon the earth.
Your friend does not desire this friendship, that those who share a common mark should become of different forms.
The heroic sons of the great Asura, the sustainers of heaven, look out widely from afar.
The immortals truly desire this from you: even the abandonment of a single mortal.
Let your mind be placed within our mind; as a husband, enter the body of your wife.
Whatever we have never done before, how could we now do it? Speaking the truth, may we never offend against untruth.
The Gandharva in the waters and the maiden who dwells therein—this is our kinship, this is our highest bond.
In the womb, the Father begot us as a husband and wife; Tvaṣṭṛ, Savitṛ, the shaper of all forms, was the god [who made us so]. No one violates his sacred laws; both Earth and Heaven know this of us.
Who knows of this first day? Who has seen it? Who here can declare it? Great is the ordinance of Mitra and Varuṇa; when will you speak to men with words of consolation?
The longing for Yama, the sister of Yama, has come upon me, that we may lie together in the same womb.
As a wife yields her body to her husband, I would yield mine; let us roll along like the wheels of a chariot.
These spies of the gods who wander here do not stand still, nor do they close their eyes.
O you who incite me to drink, go quickly with another; roll away with him like the wheels of a chariot.
May she honor him with nights and days; may the eye of Sūrya open again and again.
Yamī, who is of common kinship with Yama as heaven and earth are a pair, shall bear that which is not brother and sister.
Truly, those later ages will come when sisters shall do what is unbrotherly.
Press thy arm close to the bull; O fortunate one, seek another as thy husband.
What would a brother be if he leaves one unprotected? And what is a sister if Destruction (Nirṛti) approaches? Driven by desire, I prattle much; unite thy body with my body.
Indeed, I would not have let my body unite with your body; they call it evil when one approaches his own sister.
Arrange your pleasures with another than me; O fortunate brother, this is not what you desire.
Alas, Yama, you are truly wretched; neither your mind nor your heart have we found.
Another woman will surely embrace you, as a girth-strop encircles a harnessed horse, or as a climbing vine clings to a tree.
O Yamī, you shall embrace another, and another shall embrace you, as a climbing vine clings to a tree.
Seek his heart, or let him seek yours; then establish with him a most auspicious bond of union.
The bull has yielded for the bull the milks of heaven by his milking; the mighty one, unassailable, [is the son] of Aditi.
He knows all through his wisdom like Varuṇa; may he, the worthy of sacrifice, sacrifice according to the seasons fit for sacrifice.
The Gandharvī has uttered [her song], and the watery maiden; let her protect my mind within the roar of the river.
May Aditi place us in the midst of what is desired; may our eldest brother speak first for us.
Truly, that auspicious Dawn has shone forth for Manu—rich in food, glorious, and possessing precious wealth.
When they, according to their will, brought forth Agni as the Hotṛ priest for the sacrifice, desiring him who desires [the rite].
Then the falcon, impelled, brought down that far-reaching, all-seeing drop at the sacrifice;

when the Aryan tribes chose Agni, the wonder-worker, as their Hotṛ-priest, then the prayer was born. O Agni, you are ever delightful to the man who prospers like a pasture, you for whom the sacrifice is well-performed through the oblations of men.
Or when you, O inspired singer, having exerted yourself, approach with many [hymns] the praiseworthy strength that wins the prize;
Awaken the two parents like a lover to fortune; the beloved one desires to sacrifice and shall hasten to the heart's desire.
The bearer speaks, the sacrificer performs his work skillfully; the lord of power exerts himself and is stirred by the prayer.
O Agni, son of strength, that mortal who has attained your favor becomes renowned beyond others.
Bestowing nourishment and borne by his horses, he, radiant and protected, adorns the days.
When this divine assembly, O Agni, worthy of worship, takes place among the gods, O adorable one—
And when you, O self-dependent one, distribute treasures, grant us here our share of wealth.
Hear us, O Agni, in this common dwelling; harness your swift chariot of immortality.
Bring hither to us Heaven and Earth, the parents of the gods; let no one among the gods be absent from us here.
Heaven and Earth, first by the Eternal Law, become attentive with their truthful speech,
when the god, preparing mortals for sacrifice, sits down as the Hotṛ-priest, turning toward his own vital breath. The god,
encompassing the gods by the Eternal Law, being the first to know, carry our oblation.
He whose banner is smoke, who is kindled with fuel, the joyous invoker, eternal and most skilled in sacrifice through his voice—
when the cow’s immortal essence was won by the self-turning one, those born from it supported the two wide worlds.
All the gods followed that *yajus* of yours, whereby the heavenly water and clarified butter were milked.
I praise you both for our prosperity; O waters that drip with clarity, O Heaven and Earth, O two worlds, hear me!
Since the days have passed away without guidance, may the Father and Mother sharpen us with sweetness.
What has the King seized from us? What transgression of his law have we committed? Who knows?

For even Mitra, though he may lead the gods astray, shall be guided by the hymn; there is indeed strength in this. The name of immortality is difficult to perceive here, when that which shares a common mark becomes manifold in form. O lofty Agni, protect without fail him who meditates upon the benevolent thought of Yama.
In whom the gods rejoice at the assembly, and who maintain their station in the dwelling of Vivasvat;
they placed the light in the sun and the nights in the moon, while the two tireless ones move around the luminous orb.
In which secret thought the gods move together—we do not know this.
May Mitra, Aditi, and the god Savitṛ declare us sinless here before Varuṇa.
Hear us, O Agni, in this common dwelling; yoke your steeds...
I join you both with ancient prayer and salutations; let the hymn go forth like the path of the sun.

May all the sons of immortality hear us, they who have taken up their stations in the celestial realms. When you two came together like two Yamas striving in unison, the god-seeking men brought you forward.
Sit down in your own place, you who know it; take your seats well for our Soma juice.
I have ascended the five steps of *rūpá*; I follow the four-footed path by means of my vow. By means of the syllable (*akṣara*), I measure this out; I purify it at the navel of *ṛta*.
For the sake of the gods he chose death; for the sake of progeny he chose immortality.
They made Bṛhaspati their seer; he extended his own dear body for the sacrifice.
Seven flow for the child accompanied by the Maruts; as sons, they have established the truth for their father.
Both worlds indeed belong to him; he rules over both, and both strive for him and prosper him.
He who has gone forth along the great slopes, who has spied out the path for many— Vaivasvata, the assembler of people, Yama the king, do you honor with an oblation.
Yama was the first to find our way; this pasture-land is not to be taken away from us.
Where our ancient fathers have passed away, those who were born [to this world] following their own paths;
where Mātali with the Kavyas, Yama with the Aṅgirases, and Bṛhaspati strengthened by the Ṛkvans—
where the gods have strengthened those whom they strengthened, and where others among the gods rejoice in the *svāhā* call, while others rejoice in the *svadhā* offering.
O Yama, sit down upon this sacrificial grass, in harmony with the Aṅgirases, our ancestors.
O King, let the mantras recited by the seers bring you hither; rejoice here in the oblation.
Come with the Aṅgirases who are worthy of sacrifice; O Yama, rejoice here with the Vairūpas.
I invoke Vivasvant, who is your father, that he may sit upon the sacred grass (*barhis*) at this sacrifice.
The Aṅgirases, our fathers, the Navagvas, the Atharvans, and the Bhṛgus, who are worthy of the *soma*— may we abide in the good-will of those worthy of sacrifice, and in their auspicious benevolence.
Go forth, go forth by the ancient paths, where our former fathers have gone before us.
There you shall see both kings, rejoicing in their own power—Yama and the god Varuṇa.
Unite with the ancestors, unite with Yama, and with the merit of your sacrifices and good deeds in the highest heaven.
Leaving behind what is blameworthy, go forth again; unite with a body, O you of radiant luster.
Depart, go away, and creep far from here; for the Fathers have prepared this world for him.
Yama grants him a dwelling place, clearly distinguished by days, waters, and nights.
Run past the two dogs, the sons of Saramā, the four-eyed brindled ones, by the path of righteousness. Then go to the benevolent fathers who rejoice together with Yama in their banquet.
O Yama, those two dogs of yours who are the guardians, the four-eyed ones who watch over the path and behold men—
O King, entrust him to those two; bestow upon him well-being and freedom from disease.
The two broad-nosed, honey-colored messengers of Yama, who satisfy themselves with food, wander among the people.
May they give us back our life today so that we may behold the sun here once more, and may it be auspicious for us.
Press the Soma for Yama; offer the oblation to Yama. To Yama indeed goes the sacrifice, with Agni as its well-prepared messenger.
Offer the oblation rich in ghee to Yama and step forward.
May he grant us long life among the gods that we may live.
Offer to King Yama the most honey-sweet oblation. This homage is for the seers, the first-born, the ancient makers of the path.
It flies through the three *kadruka* cups; the six wide ones are this one great [Soma].
The *triṣṭubh*, the *gāyatrī*, and all the meters—these are all established in Yama. May the lower, the higher, and the middle *pitṛ*s, those who are worthy of the *soma*, arise!
May those who have gone to the life-breath, who are harmless and knowers of the *ṛta*, those fathers protect us in our invocations.
Let this homage be offered today to the fathers—those who went before and those who followed after;
those who are seated in the earthly realm, or those who now dwell among the well-disposed clans.
I have found the benevolent Fathers, and the grandson, and the wide stride of Viṣṇu.
Those who sit upon the sacrificial grass and partake of the pressed juice by means of the *svadhā* offering—may they come here most readily as our fathers.
O Fathers who sit upon the sacrificial grass, come hither with your aid; we have prepared these offerings for you, so please accept them.
May they come with most peaceful protection; then bestow upon us well-being and freedom from harm.
The Soma-loving ancestors have been invited to their dear offerings placed upon the sacred grass. May they come hither, may they listen here, may they speak for us, and may they protect us.
Bending your knees and sitting down to the south, may you all, O Viśve Devas, graciously accept this sacrifice.
O Fathers, do not harm us for anything; whatever offense we have committed against you through human frailty, forgive it.
Sitting in the lap of the ruddy cows, bestow wealth upon the mortal who offers oblations.
O fathers, bestow that wealth upon your sons; establish strength for them here.

Those of ours who were the ancient fathers, worthy of Soma, the Vasiṣṭhas who followed after the drinking of Soma— With them may Yama, rejoicing, desiring the offerings, eat according to his wish along with those who desire him.

RV 10.15.9: Those who have thirsted among the gods, panting, knowing the invocations, fashioning hymns with their chants—O Agni, come hither with those well-disposed, true, and wise ancestors who sit at the *gharma* vessel.
RV 10.15.10: Those who are true, eaters of the oblation, drinkers of the oblation, who are borne on the same chariot with Indra and the gods.
O Agni, come with the thousands of divine singers—both those who came before and those who followed—those ancestors who sit at the *gharma* vessel.

O Fathers consumed by fire, come here; O excellent leaders, seat yourselves each upon your respective seats. Eat the oblations presented upon the sacred grass, and then bestow upon us wealth consisting of all heroic sons.
O Agni Jātavedas, being invoked, you have carried the oblations after making them fragrant;
you have given them to the ancestors, and they have eaten them with the *svadhā* call. You, O God, have indeed consumed these presented offerings.
Those ancestors who are here and those who are not here, those whom we know and those whom we do not know—[to all of them, let this offering go].
You know how many there are, O Jātavedas; with your own offerings, enjoy the well-performed sacrifice.

Those who have been cremated by fire and those who have not, who feast upon their *svadhā* in the midst of heaven—with them, O Self-Ruler, fashion this path to the world of spirits (*asunīti*) for your body according to your will.
O Agni, do not burn him up; do not consume him with heat; do not scorch his skin or his body.
When you have made him cooked, O Jātavedas, then send him forth to the Fathers. When you have made him cooked, O Jātavedas, then...
Give him over to the fathers;
when he goes along this path of the departed, then let him become subject to the will of the gods.
Let his eye go to the sun, his breath to the wind; go to heaven and to earth according to your nature.
Go to the waters, if that is where your welfare lies; take your stand among the plants with your bodily parts.
The goat is your portion; burn it with heat; let your flame burn it, let your radiance consume it. O Jātavedas, with those forms of yours that are auspicious, carry him to the world of the righteous.
Release him again, O Agni, to the Fathers—he who, offered to you, moves with his own funeral offerings (*svadhā*).
Wearing a new life-span, let him approach his remaining kin; O Jātavedas, let him be reunited with his body.
Whatever the black bird has pecked at you, or the ant, the serpent, or even the wild beast—[may Agni purify that from you].
May Agni and Soma—who has entered into the Brahmins—make all that free from disease.
Envelop yourself with the cow-hides as Agni’s armor; cover yourself completely with fat and marrow.
Let not the bold one, exulting in his heat and seeking to seize you, encircle you with intent to consume you.
O Agni, do not overturn this cup; it is dear to the gods and to those who offer Soma.
This is the cup from which the gods drink; in it the immortal gods rejoice.
I send the flesh-eating Agni far away; let him go to the realm of Yama, carrying off the enemies.

Right here let this other Jātavedas, knowing the way, carry the oblation to the gods. The raw-flesh-eating Agni who has entered your house, seeing this other Jātavedas— him, the god, I lead away for the sacrifice to the Fathers; may he promote the Gharma offering in the highest dwelling-place.
The Agni who carries away the raw flesh, may he worship the Fathers who increase the cosmic order;
may he announce the oblations to the gods and to the Fathers. Desiring you, we set you down; desiring you, we kindle you.
Desiring them, bring the desiring ancestors here to eat the oblation.
O Agni, that which you have consumed by fire, cause that to be extinguished again; let the *kiyāmbu* grow here, and the ripe *dūrvā* grass with its spreading stalks.
O cool one, O you who possess coolness! O refreshing one, O you who possess refreshment!
Come together with the female frog and gladden this fire.
Tvaṣṭṛ prepares the bridal procession for his daughter; thus the entire world comes together.
The mother of Yama, being led away, the great wife of Vivasvat, vanished.
They concealed the immortal one from mortals; having made her of similar form, they gave her to Vivasvat.
And when that occurred, she brought forth the two Aśvins; Saraṇyū abandoned the two pairs of twins.
May Pūṣan, the wise guardian of the world whose cattle are never lost, drive you forth from here.
May he entrust you to these fathers and to Agni, who is well-disposed toward the gods.
Viśvāyu shall protect your life; may Pūṣan protect you on the distant path ahead.
Where the doers of good deeds rest, where they have gone—there may the divine Savitṛ place you.
Pūṣan knows all these regions; may he lead us by the path most free from fear.
May the giver of well-being, the glowing one, the possessor of all heroes, go before us, never failing, full of wisdom.

On the far path Pūṣan was born; on the far path of heaven, on the far path of earth. He moves hither and thither, knowing well both most beloved places of assembly. Those seeking the gods invoke Sarasvatī while the sacrifice is being performed. They invoke Sarasvatī at the unfolding of the rite.
The doers of good deeds have invoked Sarasvatī; may Sarasvatī grant what is desirable to the donor.

O Goddess Sarasvatī, you who have come on the same chariot with the Fathers, rejoicing in your own powers—having sat down upon this sacred grass (*barhis*), be exhilarated; bestow upon us food free from disease.
Sarasvatī, whom the fathers invoke as they approach the sacrifice from the south—here, bestow upon the sacrificers a portion of nourishment worth a thousand, an abundance of wealth.
May the waters, our mothers, purify us; may those who cleanse with ghee purify us with ghee.
For the divine waters carry away every stain; from them I emerge pure and cleansed.
The drop has fallen following the first days, into this womb and that which was before. I offer the drop as it moves along toward its common source, according to the seven priestly offices.
That drop of yours which spills, that stalk of yours which has fallen from the arms, from the lap of the *dhiṣaṇā* vessel;
or that which [falls] from the *adhvaryu*, or from the filter—that I offer for you with my mind, consecrated by the *vaṣaṭ* call.
That drop of yours which has spilled, that stalk of yours which has fallen down or away from the ladle.
May this divine Bṛhaspati sprinkle you for the sake of prosperity.
The plants are full of milk; full of milk is my speech.
Full of milk is the milk of the waters; with that, purify me together.
Go forth, O Death, along your own path, which is other than the way of the gods.
To you who have eyes and hear, I say this: do not harm our progeny nor our heroes.
When you have come, effacing the track of death and extending your life further, may you attain a longer span of existence.
Swelling with progeny and wealth, may you become pure, purified, and worthy of sacrifice.
These living ones have turned away from the dead; today our invocation of the gods has become auspicious.
We have gone forward for dancing and laughter, establishing a longer and more enduring life.
I set up this boundary for the living, so that no other of them may go to this goal. May they live a hundred long autumns, keeping death away by means of this mountain.
Just as days follow one after another, and as the seasons proceed duly with the seasons.
RV 10.18.5: O Ordainer, so arrange their lifespans that the later does not abandon the earlier.
RV 10.18.6: Ascend to life, choosing old age; striving together, strive in due order. May Tvaṣṭṛ, the well-born, being well-pleased, grant you long life here that you may live.

May these women, not widows and having good husbands, lie down together with ointment and clarified butter. Free from tears, free from disease, and adorned with fine jewels, let the women first ascend the bed of the deceased. Arise, O woman, toward the world of the living! Come to this one whose life has departed; come to rest beside him.
You have entered into this state of being a wife to this husband who took your hand and wooed you.

Taking the bow from the hand of the deceased, for our sovereignty, for splendor, and for strength—here indeed are you, and here are we, possessed of brave heroes; may we conquer all rivals and adversaries.
Crawl near to this mother, the earth; to the wide-extending, most gracious Pṛthivī.
Soft as wool, a young maiden to the liberal giver—may she protect you from the lap of Nirṛti.
Open wide, O Earth; do not press down upon him. Be easy of access to him, a pleasant refuge.
As a mother covers her son with the hem of her garment, so do thou, O Earth, cover him.
May the swelling Earth stand firm; let a thousand columns rise up to support her.
May those dwellings be dripping with clarified butter; may they be a refuge for him here for all time.
I prop up the earth for you; placing this dwelling around you, may I not come to harm. May the Fathers hold up this pillar for you; may Yama establish your seat here.
On the coming days, they have placed me like a leaf upon the waters.
I have seized the speech that turns back, as one holds a horse with a rein.
Turn back; do not go away. Follow us, O wealthy ones!
O Agni and Soma, you who bring back wealth, bestow riches upon us.
Bring them back again; bring them back once more.
May Indra hold them fast; may Agni drive them hither. Let them turn back again; let them thrive under this master of cattle.
Right here, O Agni, do thou maintain it; let whatever wealth there is remain right here.
That which is the path out, the path in, the meeting place, and that which is the path away; the turning toward and the turning back—him too I call upon as the guardian.

He who has brought about the departure, he who has brought about the going away—may the Guardian bring back the turning toward and the returning. Bring them back, turn them back; O Indra, give the cows back to us!
May we enjoy ourselves with the living. I bestow upon you from every side strength, ghee, and milk.
Whatever gods there are who are worthy of sacrifice, may they endow us with wealth.
O Bringer-back, turn them back; O Re-turner, turn them back!
From the four quarters of the earth, from those directions, bring them back to us. Send forth to us a gracious mind.
I praise Agni, the youngest of those who enjoy, the ruler, the friend who is difficult to resist—
the one whose law the swift-moving ones revere, [the god] from whose mother’s udder they draw forth.
Him, who dwells in the lowly nest, they magnify with their light as his banner.
The noble one shines with rows of flames; he goes forth as the path for the people when he, the seer, flashing like lightning, has reached the ends of heaven.
May he enjoy the offerings of man; standing upright, the skillful one has taken his place at the sacrifice.
Establishing the dwelling, he goes before it.
For he is the secure sacrifice of the oblation; his path proceeds with swift success.
The gods [worship] Agni, who wields the axe;
they worship Agni for the sake of sacrifice and for the attainment of bliss— the life-sustaining son of the rock, whom they call the ancient one.
May all those men who are ours be yours;
may they all increase Agni with oblations.
Black, white, and ruddy is his path; he is tawny, dappled, and red, full of glory.
The progenitor begot him of golden form.

Thus, O Agni, Vimada, being in harmony with the immortals, has brought his inspired thought to you, the Son of Strength; seeking your favor, he has offered songs of praise. You have bestowed upon us food, vigor, a secure dwelling, and all things.

We choose you as the Hotṛ priest with our own well-prepared offerings, like Agni—for the sacrifice where the sacrificial grass is strewn—at your exhilarating joy; we praise the sharp one of purifying luster.
You, indeed, these self-sustaining ones who bestow horses, adorn you.

The pouring ladle approaches you; O Agni, in your exhilaration, the straight-flying oblation is offered—you are about to speak out. Upon you the sacred laws sit with the sacrificial spoons as if pouring forth;
in your exhilaration, you assume all splendors, both dark forms and bright ones—you are about to speak out.

O Agni, O immortal one, O possessor of power, that wealth which you deem worthy—bring that to us for the winning of strength at the sacrifices; bring it, the wondrous one, in the exhilaration of the Soma; you are waxing great. Agni, born by Atharvan, has discovered all poetic wisdoms.
He became the messenger of Vivasvat; in your exhilaration, you, the beloved and desirable one of Yama, are being proclaimed aloud.
In the sacrifices, O Agni, they magnify you when the ritual proceeds;
in your exhilaration, you bestow all desirable treasures upon the donor; you are being proclaimed aloud.
RV 10.21.7: Men have established you, O Agni, as the lovely officiating priest at the sacrifices;
with your face anointed with ghee, you, the bright one, most observant, are kindled by our eyes in the exhilaration of the Soma.
RV 10.21.8: O Agni, with your bright flame, you spread yourself out widely and loftily.
Roaring aloud, you act like a bull; in your exhilaration, you place the germ within your sisters.
You wish to speak forth. Where is the famous Indra? Among which people today is he heard of as a friend?
Or is he celebrated in the dwellings of the seers, or in secret?
May Indra, heard of here, be praised among us today, the wielder of the thunderbolt, worthy of our hymns.
Like Mitra, he leads the people; he has achieved incomparable glory. He who is the lord of great power, incomparable, the impeller of great manly strength.
The wielder of the bold thunderbolt, like a father his beloved son;
harnessing the two horses of the wind, O roaring god, wielder of the thunderbolt,
you who belong to the god— speeding along the shining path, release the paths for praise.
You yourself have brought those two bay horses of Vāta to carry you;
they for whom no driver is to be found, whether god or mortal.
Now, O Uśanas, as you approach, we ask you both: "In what manner will you come to our house?"
You two have come from afar, from heaven and from earth, to the mortal man.
O Indra, you take pleasure in our offerings; our prayer is uplifted. We entreat you for that favor, so that you may slay Śuṣṇa, the human foe.
The Dasyu is without ritual action, thoughtless toward us, following alien laws, and non-human.
O slayer of enemies, strike down that Dasyu with your weapon! O Indra, you are a hero among heroes; and we, protected by you, are mighty through your power.
In many places your bounties have resounded like the peoples;
O Hero, wielder of the thunderbolt, you urged those men on in the slaying of Vṛtra and in the drawing of the sword,
when you were hidden from the seers and from the clans of star-like power.
Swiftly, O Indra, doer of great deeds, bring us those gifts, O Hero, wielder of the thunderbolt, when you have crushed Śuṣṇa and his entire brood with your companions.
O Hero Indra, let not our excellent aids be far away; may they be near to us.
O wielder of the thunderbolt, may we, each one of us, abide in the favor of these [waters].
O Indra, may those touchings of yours be true for us—touchings that are non-violent.
O wielder of the thunderbolt, may we know their enjoyment, like that of milch-cows.
When the handless and footless one grew strong through the powers of the discerning ones, you, O Indra, moving from left to right, struck down Śuṣṇa for every living being.
Drink, drink the Soma, O heroic Indra! Do not fail us, O possessor of wealth, as you are the bestower of riches.
And protect the singers and the patrons; bestow upon us great wealth and prosperity.
We worship Indra, who holds the thunderbolt in his right hand, the driver of the bay steeds that never turn back from their course.
Shaking his beard, he stands on high, showing favor with his hosts and with his bounty.
Indeed, his two bay steeds find wealth in the wood; Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, becomes the bounteous giver through his riches.
As Ṛbhu, Vāja, and Ṛbhukṣan, he rules over power; I even erase the very name of the Dāsa.
When the golden thunderbolt and the chariot come forth, which his two bay steeds draw together with the patrons.
Maghavan, renowned from of old, Indra, the lord of far-famed strength, takes his place.
Even he, the bull of the herd, together with his own, Indra, sprinkles his golden beard with rain.
He seeks the well-dwelling when the mead is pressed; he shakes it even as the wind shakes the forest.
He who with his voice struck down many thousands of the malevolent and the ill-spoken—

those very manly deeds of his we proclaim, he who, like a father, increased his power and his might. O Indra, the Vimadas have generated for you this unprecedented and most abundant hymn of praise, for the sake of the bountiful giver.
For we know the enjoyment of this mighty one, when we, like herdsmen, bring him our cattle.
Let no one sever these bonds of friendship between you, O Indra, and Vimada the son of Ṛśi.
For we know your providence, O God, as if it were that of a kinsman; may your friendships be auspicious for us.
O Indra, drink this Soma, honey-sweet, pressed in the ladle.
Bestow wealth upon us—thousandfold, O Lord of many riches—in your exhilaration; you are waxing great.
We approach you with sacrifices, with hymns, and with oblations.
O Lord of Śacī, in your exhilaration, bestow upon us the most excellent treasure among all desirable things; you are about to speak.

You who are the lord of desirable things and the impeller of the feeble, O Indra, the protector of those who praise you—in your exhilaration, guard us from our enemies and from distress; you are about to speak.

O powerful ones, you two, masters of illusion, churned apart the two united [worlds]. O Nāsatyas, when implored by Vimada, you two churned them asunder. All the gods lamented as the two united ones were being torn apart.
The gods, O Nāsatyas, said, "Bring her back again. Sweet is my departure; sweet is my return.
O you two gods, by your divine power, make our journey sweet.
May you send forth to us a blessed mind, as well as skill and wisdom.
Then, in your friendship with the soma-juice, may we rejoice in your exhilaration like cattle in a pasture; you are waxing great.
O Soma, they touch the heart in all your manifestations.
And now, in your exhilaration, these desires of ours spread abroad, seeking wealth; you shall proclaim them.
Moreover, O Soma, through my simplicity I violate your laws;
therefore, as a father toward his son, be gracious to us even from the blow of death in your exhilaration; you shall proclaim it.
Together the prayers go forth like streams from springs.
O Soma, for our life, at your exhilaration, you shall swell us like beakers; you are about to speak out.
O Soma, by your powers, these men, longing for you, have opened wide.
O Gṛtsamadha, you of great power, in your exhilaration, you wish to open wide for us the stall rich in cattle and horses.
O Soma, you protect our livestock and the moving world spread out in many places;
you bring them together that they may live, surveying all beings in your exhilaration—you wish to expand.
O Soma, be our protector from every side, one who cannot be deceived.
O King, drive away those who seek to harm us; in your exhilaration, let not the evil-minded prevail over us—you speak forth.
O Soma, you who possess excellent wisdom, be watchful for our strength and progeny.
O knower of the field, O man, in your exhilaration, protect us from the malicious one and from distress; you wax great.
O Indu, you are the most effective slayer of Vṛtra for us, the auspicious friend of Indra;
when you fight in the encounter where the lions roar, in your exhilaration, you wax great for the winning of offspring.
This indeed is that swift exhilarating drink, the beloved one, which increases the might of Indra.
This [drink] of Kakṣīvat has increased the hymn of the great sage; for your exhilaration, I shall proclaim it.
This [Soma], for the sage who offers gifts, stirs up a wealth of cattle.
At your exhilaration, he has extended [aid] better than seven [others]; may the blind and the lame walk, for you desire to speak.
For the teams of horses hasten forward toward the desirable inspired hymns. May the wondrous Pūṣan, with his team of horses, come to our aid in his greatness.
Whose greatness this mortal man has indeed attained through his vital powers—may the inspired singer win him with his prayers; he has taken note of our fair hymns.
He knows these fair hymns, like the Moon, like Pūṣan, the Bull.
He sprinkles the nourishing food; he sprinkles it for us like a stall. May we honor you, O divine Pūṣan;
may we honor you as the fulfiller of our thoughts and the protector of the sages.
The horse that speeds the chariots is the counterpart of the sacrifice; he is the seer who is established as Manu, the friend who drives away the enemy of the sage.
He is the lord of her who studies, of the sorrowful woman, and of the pure man.
The one who wears the raiment of sheepskins has cleansed his garments.
The lord of spoils, the master of nourishments, the friend of prosperity—
he, the beloved, whose beard he shakes, he who is invincible, lets his hair flow loose.
O Pūṣan, may the goats turn the pole of your chariot;
you are the friend of every seeker, born of old and unshakable.
May the mighty Pūṣan protect our chariot with nourishing strength.
Be the strengthener of those who offer oblations; may he hear this our invocation.

O singer, let it be well with me when I bestow my aid upon the sacrificer who presses the Soma. I am the slayer of him who offers no blessing, the one who strikes down the deceiver who walks in crooked ways.

If I were to lead out for battle those who seek the gods and have exerted themselves with their bodies—then, O Bull, I would cook for you at home a powerful bull; I would pour out the sharp, pressed juice, fifteenfold.
I do not know him who says, "It was I who slew the god-seekers in the encounter."
When he announced the battle, the fierce one roared; then indeed the bulls began to speak aloud.
While I was among unknown tribes, all the wealthy lords were mine. Whether I conquer one who is at ease, or seize him by the foot on the mountain, I strike down that destroyer.
Indeed, they do not hold me back in the struggle, nor do the mountains, when I set my mind upon it.
At my roar, the short-eared one shall be afraid; even from afar, the scatterer shall tremble day after day.
Behold here those who drink the cooked [milk], who are without Indra, who feed on their own arms, and who tremble before the arrow.
RV 10.27.6: May the fellies of the chariot turn back upon those who have reviled our joyful friend.

RV 10.27.7: You have become manifest; you have extended life. The former has indeed burst forth, and the latter shall burst forth. Two garments encompass him who has reached the further limit of this space.
The cows of the nobleman have eaten the barley in great numbers; I saw them wandering together with their herdsman.
The enemies have come together from all sides; how much longer will the master of the house let them go unpunished?
When we, the grass-eaters among men, and I, the barley-eater within the wide stall, come together—
9. Here, when yoked, he shall seek one who would unyoke him; and having spoken, he shall unyoke the one who is not yet yoked.

10. Right here you shall consider my word as truthfully spoken: I shall unite the bipeds and the quadrupeds. Whoever here, with women, attacks the bull in battle—though he be without a fight—I shall divide his wealth.
Whose daughter was once eyeless—what man, knowing this, would desire her who is blind?
Which of the two shall release the arrow: he who carries her away, or he who shall woo her?
How great is the maiden, the bride of a mortal, who is so highly esteemed by the noble suitor?
The bride becomes auspicious when she is well-adorned; she herself chooses her husband even among the people.
The foot has swallowed him; he eats facing backward; with his head he has placed a head upon himself as a protection.
Sitting, he destroys the upright woman in his lap; he follows the supine woman down to the earth.
High and shadowless, leafless, the steed stood; the mother, released, devoured the embryo.
Licking the calf of another, she lowed; in what world did the cow set down her udder?
Seven heroes rose up from below; eight from above came together.
Nine from behind have come forth, possessing pillars; ten from the front traverse the ridge, eating.
Of the ten, one tawny one is common to them all; they urge him on for the sake of noble power.
The mother bears the well-placed embryo within her womb, lulling it to sleep while she herself does not tire.
The heroes cooked a fat ram; the dice were cast and played for the game. Two [streams] flow through the waters, possessing wide vessels and purifying filters, cleansing themselves.
Crying out, they went in all directions; one half shall cook, for the other half shall not cook.

This god Savitṛ has declared this to me: "He who feeds on wood shall win it; he who feeds on clarified butter shall win it. I saw a village being carried away from afar, revolving by its own inherent power without wheels.
The noble one follows the generations of men, instantly destroying the phalluses as a newer one.
These two oxen of Pramaras, yoked for me—do not drive them away; let them trample him repeatedly.
Even the waters shall fail his purpose, and the sun shall become a destroyer for him.
This thunderbolt, which has been hurled in many ways from beneath the mass of the great Sun—
Beyond this there is another thing called fame; through it, they overcome old age without distress.
Bound to every tree, the cow lowed; from there the man-eating birds flew forth.
Then this entire world was struck with fear; let him bestow gifts upon the one who presses the Soma for Indra and the seer.
The first ones stood in the dwelling of the gods; they went upward from the lower world, cutting away the evil. Three heat the earth from below; two carry the swelling moisture.
This is your life-sustenance; know that for yourself. Do not hide such a thing from me in the assembly.
The sheep makes the sun its own and hides the dust; though it is manifest, it is not released from its dark covering.
Every other kinsman has come away, but my father-in-law here has not gone away.
May he eat the food and drink the Soma; well-fed, may he go back home again.
Roaring like a bull with sharpened horns, he stands upon the height, over the breadth of the earth. "In all these gatherings, I protect him who fills my belly with pressed soma.
With the stone, O Indra, they quickly press for you exhilarating soma juices; you drink of them.
They cook bulls for you; you eat of them, O Maghavan, when you are invoked with nourishing food.
O singer, understand this well for me: the rivers carry their curse back against themselves. The fox has devoured the lion as he came toward him; the jackal has driven the boar out from the thicket.
How could I, an unripe one, understand this inspired thought of yours, O wise and powerful Soma?
You, being the knower, must declare to us according to the seasons that side which, O Maghavan, is the secure path.
For thus they magnify me, the powerful; even higher than the great heaven is my path.
I sharpen many thousands all at once, for my progenitor begot me without a rival.
For thus indeed have the gods known me, Indra, as powerful, fierce, and virile in every deed.
Exulting, I slew Vṛtra with the thunderbolt; by my greatness, I opened the cow-stall for the donor.
The gods came, carrying axes; felling the forests, they approached with their tribes. They placed the well-rolling [fire] within the bellies [of the trees], where they burn along with the dry wood.
The hare swallowed the razor as it faced him; from afar, he split the mountain with a clod of earth.
I shall subject even the great to the small; like a calf growing strong, let it overcome the bull.
The eagle has thus struck its claw; the lion, hemmed in, has reached the trap.
Though the buffalo is thirsty and trapped, let the leather thong drag him away from there.

The iguana shall drag away by the feet those who, with their food, seek to obstruct the sacred word (*brahman*). They themselves devour the bulls that have been let loose, while they crush their own bodies.
These men have become truly well-performing through their labors, who have impelled their bodies with Soma-hymns.
Speaking like a man, bestow upon us great strengths; you have established your name as a hero in heaven.
Like one placed within a wood, he has shone forth; the pure hymn has awakened you two, O impetuous ones.
He whose Hotar-priest is Indra through many days—he who is the protector of men, most heroic among heroes, the lord of the night.
May we be yours at the dancing of this dawn and of the future one, O most heroic of heroes.
May the chariot of Triśoka, which has been victorious, bring a hundred men along with Kutsa. What exhilaration is pleasing to you, O Indra? Being fierce, run forth toward the doors and our songs.
When will my inspired thought come hither to you, O Bearer? May I be able to bring you near with gifts of food.
What is the glory of one like you, O Indra, among men? With what intention do you act? Why have you not come to us?
Like Mitra, you are true, O Wide-strider; for our sustenance, let all our inspired thoughts be directed toward your food.
Drive them away like the sun toward its goal, those who have come to his desire like those seeking a wife.
And those men, O Indra of many births, who with food strive to win back your many songs of praise.
For you, O Indra, two well-measured mothers exist: the vast sky by your majesty, and the earth by your wisdom.

For your choice, let these pressed juices mixed with ghee and sweet honey be most pleasant for your drinking. They have poured out a full vessel of honeyed mead for this Indra, for he is truly bountiful in his gifts.
He has grown great upon the wide expanse of the earth, preeminent through his wisdom and manly deeds.
Indra, self-strong, has overwhelmed the hostile armies; many [people] strive for his friendship.
Mount him as you would a chariot in battles—him whom you shall urge on with auspicious and gracious favor.
May the path toward the gods proceed to the Brahmin; let it go forth toward the waters by the impulse of the mind.
I have offered this great, well-fashioned hymn as a nourishing draught for Mitra and Varuṇa, whose course is wide.
O Adhvaryus, be provided with oblations; desiring them, come hither toward the longing waters.
With skillful hands, press down today that wave which the ruddy, fair-winged bird gazes upon.
O Adhvaryus, go to the waters, to the ocean; worship the Son of the Waters with an oblation. May he grant you a well-purified wave today; for him, press out the honeyed Soma.
He who shines within the waters without being kindled, whom the sages invoke at the sacrifices.
O Son of the Waters, grant us the honey-sweet waters, those by which Indra was strengthened for heroic power.
Those with which Soma rejoices and exults, like a noble youth with beautiful maidens— O Adhvaryu, go toward those waters; when you pour them out, purify them with the plants.
Even so do the young maidens bow down to the youth, when he, desiring them, approaches them who desire him. They agree in mind, they are of one accord—the Adhvaryus and the divine Dhiṣaṇās.
He who made room for you when you were obstructed, he who released you from great calumny—[to him, O Soma, flow].
O Waters, send forth for that Indra a honeyed wave, a delighter of the gods. Send forth for him a honeyed wave, which is your embryo, O rivers, and a fountain of sweetness.
O wealthy Waters, hear my call—the one who is smeared with ghee, worthy of praise at the sacrifices.
O rivers, send forth that exhilarating wave, the drink of Indra, which sets both worlds in motion— that fountain, the source of intoxication,
born of the clouds, longing for the waters, moving through the triple-threaded filter. Now they flow back again in two streams, like those who fight for cattle, wandering toward the settled dwelling.
O Sage, pay homage to the Waters, the mothers of the seer and wives of the world, who increase our prosperity and share a common origin.
Further our sacrifice for the worship of the gods; further our prayer so that it may win riches.
Unbind your udders at the yoking of the *ṛta*; O Waters, be gracious hearers unto us.
O wealthy Waters, you indeed rule over riches; you bear within yourselves auspicious wisdom and immortality.
You are the mistresses of wealth consisting of noble offspring; may Sarasvatī grant that vitality to the one who praises her.
When the Waters are seen approaching, carrying clarified butter, milk, and honey—
In mental harmony with the *adhvaryu* priests, they bring the well-pressed *soma* for Indra.
These wealthy ones have come, bestowing life; O *adhvaryu*s, friends, set them down!
O you who are worthy of *soma*, place them upon the sacred grass (*barhis*), being in accord with these, the offspring of the waters.
The longing waters have come to this sacred grass; seeking the gods, they have settled at our sacrifice.
O Adhvaryus, press the Soma for Indra; your worship of the gods has now become easy to perform.
May the praiseworthy invocation of the gods come to us for our protection, with all the swift ones, O worthy of sacrifice.
Through these [songs], may we be good friends; crossing over all difficulties, may we remain so.
A mortal should indeed reflect upon wealth and seek to win it through the path of *ṛta* with reverence.
Therefore, he should consult with his own wisdom and grasp a better resolve with his mind.

The prayer has been established; the portions have been released. Like [gifts] at a ford, the offerings go toward the Wondrous One. We have attained the strength of prosperity; we have become aware of the immortals.
May the eternal Lord of the House, the giver of gifts, for whom the god Savitṛ has begotten [this wealth], find pleasure in us;
may Bhaga or Aryaman adorn him with cattle, and may he, like a sacrificial vessel, provide him with splendor and be his protector.
May this [house] become like the dwelling of the Dawns, when those possessing food come together in their might.
Seeking the praise of this singer, may strengthening gains come to us.
This benevolence of his has spread wide; from of old it was like the earth. They dwell together in the womb of the Asura, moving about in common within the same support.
What was the wood, and what was that tree, from which they fashioned heaven and earth? Firmly established, undecaying, and swift-acting, they endure; many days and many dawns have worn away.
There is nothing else beyond these two; he, the bull, supports both heaven and earth.
The self-dependent one makes for himself that purifier when his bay steeds carry him like the sun.
Like a steed he traverses the broad earth; like the wind, he scatters the mist over the ground.
Where Mitra and Varuṇa are anointed, Agni has released his splendor like [fire] in the forest.
The barren cow, being suddenly impregnated, brought forth; the trembling one made herself free from trembling, having found her own protector.
When the first son was born from his parents, the ox swallowed the sacrificial pin—so they say, if one should ask.
And they call Kaṇva the son of Nṛṣad; moreover, the dark-brown steed won the prize.
For the dark one, the bright udder overflowed; no one else caused it to swell for him here.
May the two who go forth, the companions of the one who meditates, sit down among the choicest gifts, bestowing boons upon the seekers.
O Indra, may you enjoy both of our offerings when you take notice of the Soma juice.
O Indra, much-praised one, you traverse the celestial luminaries and the earthly realms with your radiance.
May those who repeatedly bring you to the sacrifices, bestowing wealth upon us, be further impelled by our prayers.
May that be more wondrous than the wonder itself: that a son, having been born, should take up the knowledge from his parents.
The wife leads her husband with her voice; well-prepared with men, the auspicious bridal procession has set out.
I have meditated upon that lovely common dwelling-place, where the cows lowed like milch-cows for the bridal procession.
When the Mother, the primal one of the herd, the sevenfold source of song, and the people gathered together.
One who seeks the gods has surpassed your station; alone among the Rudras, he goes forth as a conqueror.

Pour out the honeyed draught for those immortal ones through whom old age is granted as a gift. That which was being deposited, hidden within the waters—the guardian of the gods' laws has declared it to me.

Indra, the knower, has indeed beheld you; instructed by him, O Agni, I have come here. One who does not know the field has asked the one who knows the field; he, instructed by the one who knows the field, has gone forward.
This indeed is the auspicious instruction; furthermore, he finds the direct path among the winding ways.
Today indeed has this breathing creature come to eat; hitherto it has been covered, yet now it sucks at its mother’s udder.
Old age has approached this youth; he has become gracious, benevolent, and free from anger.
O Kalaśa, we have performed these auspicious deeds for you, O Kurushravas, as you bestow gifts.
RV 10.32.9: O bounteous ones, let that gift be yours; and this Soma which I bear within my heart [is yours].
RV 10.33.1: The harnesses of men have yoked me forward; I carry Pūṣan between [the worlds].
All the gods protected me then; the cry arose, "The evil-minded one has come!"
My ribs pain me on all sides like rival wives;
exhaustion oppresses me, and nakedness afflicts me; my mind trembles like one who is hungry.
O Śatakratu, the worms devour me, even as they eat the singer of your praises.
O Maghavan Indra, be gracious to us once; then, be to us like a father.
I, the seer, have chosen King Kuruśravaṇa, the son of Trasadasyu, the most generous among those who offer oblations.
He whose three bay horses carry me straightway in his chariot—
[I praise him] at the sacrifice where a thousand-fold dakṣiṇā is given.
The songs of Upamaśravas’s father are as sweet as nectar.
They called it a field of delight for the one who speaks;
O Upamaśravas, come as a son to the grandson of Mitrātithi;
here, at this sacrifice, is the praise of your father.
If I were the lord of the immortals or even of mortals, my liberal patron would live for a hundred autumns. No one lives beyond the decree of the gods, not even one who possesses a hundred lives.
Thus, with an even number [of nuts], they have turned away.
The *prāvepa* fruits of the great tree exhilarate me, growing in the windy place and rolling upon the gaming board.
Like a draught of Soma from Mount Mujavat, the wakeful *vibhīdaka* nut has appeared before me.

She did not scold me, nor was she angry; she was kind to my friends and to me. For the sake of a single throw of the die, I have driven away my devoted wife. My mother-in-law hates me, and my wife holds me back; though I am in distress, I find no one to comfort me.
Like the carcass of an aged horse for sale, I find no enjoyment at all in this gambler.
Others caress the wife of him whose wealth the die has coveted. His father, mother, and brothers say of him: "We do not know him; lead him away bound."
When I thought, "I shall not play with these," I was left behind by my departing friends.
And when the brown dice were cast, they raised their voices; their movement was like that of a mistress to her lover.
The gambler goes to the assembly hall asking questions, his body trembling as he thinks, "I shall win."
The dice further his desire; they bestow winnings upon the opponent. The dice indeed are barbed, piercing, deceitful, burning, and scorching.
RV_10.034.07.2 They grant gifts like children; they conquer and strike back again, mingled with honey through the power of the gambler.

RV_10.034.08.1 A troop of fifty-three plays with them, like the god Savitṛ whose laws are true. RV_10.034.08.2 Even before the wrath of the fierce one, they bow down; even the king himself pays homage to them.
Bent low, yet flickering upward, the handless dice overcome the man who has hands.
Like divine coals cast upon the gambling-ground, though cold themselves, they burn the heart to ashes.
The gambler’s wife is distressed at being abandoned; the mother grieves for her son as he wanders who knows where.
Owing a debt and fearing, yet desiring wealth, he goes to the home of others at nightfall.
Having seen another's wife, the gambler is tormented by her and by that well-made dwelling.
In the forenoon he yoked his brown horses, but at the end of the day, the wretched man fell down by the fire.

He who has become the commander of your great host, the king of the multitude, the foremost of the troop—to him I pay homage; I do not withhold wealth from him for ten days; I speak this as the truth.
Do not play with dice; practice agriculture; take delight in your possessions, regarding them as much.
There are your cows, O gambler; there is your wife. This Aryaman Savitar reveals it to me.
Make friends with us; indeed, be merciful to us. Do not approach us with your terrible and impetuous wrath. Let your anger and hostility now depart; let another fall into the snare of the brown dice.
Those fires, accompanied by Indra, have awakened; bearing light at the dawning of the Uṣas, may the great Heaven and Earth take notice. Today we choose for ourselves the protection of the gods.
We choose the protection of Heaven and Earth, of the mother rivers, the mountains, and the Śaryaṇāvat.
We pray to Sūrya and Uṣas for freedom from sin; may the well-pressed Soma bring us good fortune today.
May the two great Mothers, Heaven and Earth, protect us today from sin for our welfare.
May the dawning Dawn drive away evil; we pray for the well-being of the kindled Agni.
May this first Dawn, auspicious for the gods, rich in wealth, shine forth riches for us who seek gain.

May we keep far away the wrath of the malevolent; we pray to the kindled Agni for well-being. Those Dawns which stream forth with the rays of the Sun, bringing light at their break of day—may they dawn upon us.
May auspicious light shine upon us today for our renown; we pray for the well-being of the kindled Agni. May the Uṣases come to us free from disease; may the fires rise up with lofty light.
May the Aśvins yoke their swift chariot; we pray for the well-being of the kindled Agni.
O Savitṛ, impel for us today that most excellent and desirable portion; for you are the bestower of jewels.
I address Dhiṣaṇā, the mother of wealth; we pray to the well-kindled Agni for well-being.
May that proclamation of the Truth (Ṛta) fulfill me—that which belongs to the gods, as we mortals have conceived it.
The sun rises, beholding all the rays of light; we pray for well-being to Agni as he is kindled.
Free from hatred today, as the sacred grass is strewn, we pray for the success of our thought during the harnessing of the pressing-stones.
You stand within the protection of the Ādityas, O active one; we pray for well-being to Agni as he is kindled.
I invite the gods to our great sacrificial grass at the common feast in heaven; I seat the seven Hotṛ-priests.
For our gain, we pray for Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, Bhaga, and the well-kindled Agni for our well-being.
O Ādityas, come hither for our complete prosperity; with one accord, protect our sacrifice for our increase.

We pray to Bṛhaspati, Pūṣan, the Aśvins, Bhaga, and the well-kindled Agni for well-being. O Ādityas, O Gods, grant us that which is worthy of proclamation: a shelter that is well-sustained and protects our men.
For our cattle, our children, our progeny, and for life itself, we pray to the well-kindled Agni for well-being.
May all the Maruts come today with every aid; may all the fires be kindled.
May all the gods come to us with protection; may all wealth and strength be ours.
O gods, whomsoever you favor in the struggle for booty, whomsoever you protect, and whomsoever you deliver from distress—[him we invoke].
He who knows no fear under your protection—may we be such as he for the feast of the gods, O swift ones!

Dawn and Night, the lofty and well-adorned; Heaven and Earth, Varuṇa, Mitra, and Aryaman—I invoke Indra, the Maruts, the mountains, the waters, the Ādityas, Heaven and Earth, the waters, and the light of heaven.
May Heaven and Earth, the wise ones who follow the cosmic order (*ṛta*), protect us from distress and from injury.
May Nirṛti, the goddess of misfortune, who is hard to perceive, have no power over us; we choose today that protection of the gods.
May Aditi, the mother of Mitra and of wealthy Varuṇa, protect us from every distress.
May we attain that light which wins the sun and is free from predators—of the gods...
May the pressing-stone, speaking aloud, drive away the demons, evil dreams, Nirṛti, and every devouring fiend.
May we attain the protection of the Ādityas and the Maruts—of the gods...
May Indra sit upon the sacrificial grass; may the *iḷā* overflow; may Bṛhaspati, the seer of Ṛks, sing with the Sāmans.
May we fashion a well-awakened prayer for life—this [is] of the gods... O Aśvins, make our sacrifice touch the heavens, quicken the rite, and grant us favor for the sacrifice.
RV 10.36.6.2: That which has been offered with ghee, with its rays directed eastward—that of the gods...
RV 10.36.7.1: I invoke the host of Maruts, who are easy to call upon, purifying, lofty, and bringing prosperity for our friendship.
RV 10.36.7.2: May we obtain an increase of wealth for the sake of high renown—that of the gods...

We bring forth the drinker of waters, the source of life, the protector of the gods, easy to invoke, the glory of the sacrifice—the Soma of bright rays, the power of Indra; may we attain that which belongs to the gods.
May we, as living men with living sons, being free from sin, win that through our skillful gains by means of our acquisitions.
May those who hate the *brahman* be carried away in every direction by their own sin; that is the power of the gods...
O you who are worthy of Manu’s sacrifice, listen! O gods, grant us that which we implore from you:
a victorious will, wealth, and glory accompanied by heroic sons; that is the power of the gods...
Today we choose for ourselves the great protection of the great gods, the lofty ones who are invincible.
So that we may obtain wealth born of heroes, may we attain that [favor] of the gods. In the shelter of the greatly kindled Agni, may we be sinless before Mitra and Varuṇa for our well-being.
May we abide in the most excellent impulsion of Savitṛ; that [is] the portion of the gods...
All those gods who are under the ordinance of Savitṛ, whose impulsion is true, and of Mitra and Varuṇa— Do you bestow upon us prosperity consisting of heroes and cattle, and wonderful wealth.
Savitar from behind, Savitar from the front, Savitar from above, Savitar from below—may Savitar impel all prosperity for us; may Savitar grant us long life.
Homage to the eye of Mitra and Varuṇa! To the great god, offer this *ṛta*.
Sing praises to Sūrya, the son of Dyaus, who is visible from afar, born of the gods, and the banner of light.
May this word of truth protect me on every side, as far as Heaven and Earth have spread out the days.
Everything else that moves goes to rest, but the waters flow forever and Sūrya rises for all time.
No godless man from of old can stay thy path when thou dost speed along with thy winged coursers.
One region follows after thee as thou movest forward, O Sūrya, with thy light from above.
With that light, O Sūrya, wherewith thou drivest away the darkness, thou risest up for the whole world with thy radiance.
By that [means], drive away from us all lack of food, the failure of our oblation, disease, and evil dreams.
For, dispatched, you guard the law of every [being]; unangered, you rise up according to your own inherent power (*svadhā*).
O Sūrya, whatever resolve we declare to you today, may the gods favor that intention of ours.
May Heaven and Earth, may the Waters, Indra, and the Maruts hear this our invocation and this our word.
May we not be deprived of the sight of the sun; living auspiciously, may we reach old age.
May we always have a gracious mind and clear vision, possessing offspring, free from disease, and sinless.
O Sūrya, you whose splendor is like that of Mitra, may we, living long, behold you rising day after day.
O far-seeing one, bearing great light, radiant and a source of joy for every eye,
may we, while yet alive, behold you as you ascend from the vast expanse of heaven.
O Sūrya, golden-haired one, by whose signal all beings move forth and by whose rays they return to rest, grant us, day after day, greater and greater sinlessness through your auspiciousness.
Be a blessing to us with your eye, a blessing to us with the day, a blessing with your light, a blessing with your coolness, and a blessing with your heat.
RV 10.37.10: Just as there is peace on the path and peace within this dwelling, O Sūrya, bestow upon us manifold wealth.
RV 10.37.11: O Gods, grant protection to both our classes of people—to our bipeds and our quadrupeds.
May they eat and drink with vigor; having been satisfied, bestow upon us that health, prosperity, and freedom from harm.
O Gods, whatever grievous offense we have committed against you with our tongue or through a lapse of mind that incurs your wrath—
O Vasus, lay that sin upon him who, being ungenerous, seeks to bring misfortune upon us. O Indra, protect us in this glorious battle, in this fierce and tumultuous clamor, so that we may prevail.
Where, in the fierce struggle for cattle among the bold and armored warriors, the missiles fly in every direction to win men;
O Indra, in that place of battle, disclose to us wealth abounding in food and surging with cattle, a fame-worthy treasure.
O Śakra, may we be your allies as you conquer; O Vasu, do that which we desire.

O Indra, much-praised one, whether it be a Dāsa or an Ārya who intends to challenge us to battle, may those enemies be easy for us to overcome with you; may we, through you, conquer them in the encounter. He who is to be invoked by few and he who is to be invoked by many—he who finds room for us in the close combat of manly strife.
Today we bring hither for our protection Indra, the famous hero, the winner in the fray, who comes toward us.
For I have heard, O Indra, that you are self-guiding, the driver away of the foe, the bull who impels the weak.
Release yourself from Kutsa; come here! How can one like you remain bound by the testicles?

O Aśvins, that well-rolling chariot of yours which travels around the earth, to be invoked at evening and at dawn by those who offer oblations— that very chariot of yours, ever-present, we now invoke, easy to call upon, as if calling upon our father.
Impel our truthful words; swell our inspired thoughts; send forth our abundant wisdom—that is what we desire.
O Aśvins, grant us a glorious portion; make our Soma dear to the liberal patrons.
Though you are not aged, you become our fortune; you are the protectors even of the most destitute.
O Nāsatyas, they call you the physicians of the weak, of the emaciated, and even of the sick.

You two fashioned Cyavāna, who was worn out like an old chariot, into a youth again for the sake of movement. You carried Tugra’s son out from the waters; all these deeds of yours are to be proclaimed at the Soma-pressings. Your ancient heroic exploits are to be told among the people; thus you have acted as physicians, bringingers of well-being.
RV 10.39.5: Let us now perform these new deeds for your protection, O Nāsatyas, so that the enemy may have no faith.

RV 10.39.6: I call upon you both; hear me, O Aśvins. Like parents to their son, grant me your aid. I am without kin, unknown, and without a clan, lacking intelligence. Before this curse reaches me, deliver me from it!
On your chariot you brought Śundhyū, the daughter of Purumitra, to Vimada.
You came to the call of Vadhrimatī; you brought forth good offspring for Purandhi.
You restored the youthful vigor of the sage Kali, who had reached old age.
You two rescued Vandana from the jaws of the wild beast; you two instantly enabled Viśpalā to run.
O Aśvins, O bulls, you two brought forth Rebha, who was hidden in a cave and deprived of his senses. You two restored the heated cauldron to Atri, providing him with vital breath for Saptavadhri.
O Aśvins, you gave to Pedu a white horse, powerful with ninety-nine new strengths—
a horse worthy of praise, swift-moving, a friend, a source of fortune for men, one to be invoked, and a bringer of bliss. O Kings,
neither from any quarter nor from anywhere does distress, misfortune, or fear reach that man whom you protect, O Aditi.
O Aśvins, you who are easy to invoke and whose path is red with light, you place the chariot in front together with its wife.

Come hither on that chariot which is swifter than thought, which the R̥bhus fashioned for you, O Aśvins— the chariot at the harnessing of which Heaven’s daughter is born, and both fair days of Vivasvat arise.
Come along the path with your victorious [chariot] across the mountain; you made the cow Śayavī swell with milk, O Aśvins.
Even from the jaws of the wolf, you released by your wondrous powers the quail that had been swallowed.
O Aśvins, we have fashioned this hymn for you, just as the Bhṛgus fashioned a chariot.
We have embraced you as a young woman embraces her lover, bearing you like one bears an eternal son.
Where is your chariot going, O Heroes? Who indeed honors your radiant presence for our well-being?
It travels at dawn, all-pervading, borne day after day by prayer and ritual labor for the sake of every clan.
Where indeed are you at night? Where during the day, O Aśvins? Where do you go toward us? Where have you stayed?

Who brings you to his dwelling, as a widow brings her brother-in-law, or as a young woman brings her lover? You two awaken at dawn like two aged women; O worshipful ones, you come to the house at every dawn.
Whose [offerings] do you destroy, or for whom, O heroes, do you go to the libations like two princes?
