Like powerful heroes, worthy of praise, destroyers of enemies, noble men, they reach toward the heavens.
At your foundation, as if on the course of the waters, the earth trembles and yields.
This all-nourishing sacrifice is turned toward you; come hither like those who provide nourishment at a constant feast.
You are like yoke-horses with their reins, radiant with light at the break of dawn;

like hawks, you are self-glorious destroyers of enemies; like travelers on a journey, you are far-reaching and pervasive. When you, O Maruts, come forth from afar, you bring great wealth from the vast enclosure.
Knowing what is to be attained, O Vasus, drive far away our enemies.

The man who, at the conclusion of the sacrifice, stands firm in the rites and offers gifts to the Maruts—may he possess abundant wealth and heroic sons; may he be the one who dwells in the protection of the gods.
For they are the ones worthy of sacrifice at the rites, the helpers who bring most perfect well-being by their name, "the Ādityas.
May they protect our prayer that speeds on the chariot, they who take delight in the great majesty of the sacrifice.
Like inspired poets with their hymns, these gods are well-disposed; like those who seek the gods with sacrifices, they are easily won.
Like kings, they are brilliant and beautiful to behold; they are the lords of the people, blameless and worthy of homage.
Like fire with its radiance, they wear golden ornaments upon their breasts; like winds that yoke themselves, they provide immediate aid.
Like the eldest among those who know the way, they are excellent leaders; like Soma juices, they grant good protection to the one who follows the *ṛta*.
Like winds that are shakers and swift-moving, they are radiant like the tongues of fires;

like warriors clad in armor, they are vigorous; like the praises of the Fathers, they are bounteous givers. Like the spokes of chariots joined at the hub, they are victorious; like heroes, they look toward heaven.
Like bridegrooms seeking a wife, they sprinkle clarified butter; like singers of hymns, they chant the *arkas* beautifully.
Like the finest horses, they are swift; like chariot-riders, they are bounteous givers.
Moving forward with waters like rivers flow down slopes, they are multiform, like the *Aṅgirases* with their *sāmans*.
Like pressing-stones are the wise ones, sons of Sindhu, ever-shattering like rocks;
like playful children with good mothers, they are a great host on their march, and [they shine] with splendor.
Like the banners of the dawns, they are the ornaments of the sacrifice; seeking beauty, they have shone forth with ointments.
Like flowing rivers with gleaming spears, they have measured out their courses from afar across many leagues.
O Maruts, you who are ever-increasing, make us fortunate and richly endowed with jewels, we who are your praisers.
Remember our hymn and our friendship; for since of old there have been gifts of treasure from you.
I have beheld the greatness of this great one, the immortality of the immortal among mortal clans.
His jaws, spread apart, come together; insatiable, devouring, they consume much food.
His head is placed in secret; his eyes are directed straight ahead; insatiable, he eats the forests with his tongue.
Here they bring together for him the protections with their feet; with uplifted hands, they pay homage to him among the people.
Seeking his mother’s secret, most distant place, he has glided through the wide plants like a child.
He has found him, glowing and licking the raw flesh within the lap of the earth, as if it were ripe food.
I proclaim that truth to you both, O Heaven and Earth: as soon as he is born, the embryo devours his two parents.
As a mortal, I do not understand the god; only Agni, truly, is wise and all-knowing.
He who zealously offers us food, who sacrifices with clarified butter and ghee, and nourishes him—[him does Agni favor].
He beholds with a thousand eyes; O Agni, you face every direction.
What offense have you committed against the gods, O Agni? I ask you now, being ignorant.
Playing or not playing, the tawny one has eaten for his meal; he has cut [the wood] joint by joint like a knife through a cow.
He who is born of the wood has yoked his horses that rush in all directions, held fast by straight-tightening reins.
Well-born Mitra, together with the Vasus, has shared out [the portions]; increasing, he has grown strong through his joints.
Agni bestows the prize-winning steed; Agni bestows the hero renowned for his steadfastness in action.
Agni moves between the two worlds, anointing them; Agni [stirs] the woman Purandhi, whose womb holds heroes.
May there be auspicious fuel for Agni, the active one; Agni has entered the two great worlds.
Agni impels the solitary man in battles; Agni shatters many Vṛtras.
Agni indeed protected Tyajaratkarṇa; Agni burned Jarūtha out from the waters.
Agni rescued Atri within the heat; Agni united Nṛmedha with progeny.
Agni has granted wealth adorned with heroes; Agni [grants it] to the seer who wins thousands.
Agni has extended the oblation to heaven; the domains of Agni are distributed in many places.
The seers invoke Agni with hymns; men, unoppressed, call upon Agni on their journey.
Birds flying in the mid-air [seek] Agni; Agni goes around thousands of cattle.
The human tribes that have sprung from Manu and Nahuṣa invoke Agni;
Agni [invokes] the Gandharva-path of the Cosmic Order (ṛta); Agni’s pasture is established in clarified butter.
For Agni the Ṛbhus fashioned a prayer; we have uttered a great hymn of praise to Agni.
O Agni, youngest god, protect the singer; O Agni, win for us great wealth through sacrifice.
The seer who, as Hotṛ-priest, sat down as our father, offering up all these worlds— he, seeking wealth through his prayer, entered the lower regions as the first to cover them.
What was the foundation? What was the starting point? What was its support? From what did Viśvakarman, who generates the earth and by his greatness uncovers the sky, being all-seeing, [proceed]?
He whose eye is everywhere, whose face is everywhere, whose arms are everywhere, and whose feet are everywhere—[he alone is the creator].
The one God, generating heaven and earth, welds them together with his arms and wings.
What was the wood and what was that tree from which they fashioned forth heaven and earth? O wise ones, ask this in your minds: upon what did he stand while supporting the worlds?

Those which are your highest abodes, those which are lowest, and those which are intermediate, O Viśvakarman—teach these to your friends at the oblation, O self-dependent one; strengthening yourself, sacrifice for your own body.
O Viśvakarman, strengthened by the oblation, sacrifice for yourself upon the earth and the sky.
Let other people around us be bewildered; here, let our patron be our benefactor.
Today, for our protection in the struggle for booty, we shall invoke Viśvakarman, the Lord of Speech, who is swift as thought.
May he, the source of all well-being and the performer of righteous deeds, graciously accept all our invocations for our aid.

The Father of the eye, wise in his mind, created these two worlds as they were being measured out, with clarified butter as their food. When the eastern boundaries were firmly established, then Heaven and Earth spread themselves out.
Viśvakarman, the far-reaching one of vast intellect, is the Ordainer, the Disposer, and the supreme Seer.
Their sacrifices rejoice in nourishment where they say there is one beyond the seven seers.
He who is our father and progenitor, he who is the ordainer and knows all abodes and all worlds—he alone is the sole name-giver of the gods; to him all other worlds go for instruction.
The ancient seers, the singers, the sons of *nabhas*, performed sacrifices for him to win wealth together— those who, seated in the unmanifested and manifested space, created all these beings.
That which exists beyond heaven, beyond this earth, and beyond the gods and the *asuras*...

What was the first embryo that the waters received, wherein all the gods were beheld together? That very embryo the waters received as the first, wherein all the gods came together; it was placed upon the navel of the Unborn, in which all worlds abide.
You do not know him who generated these [worlds], that which has become the innermost part of you.
Enveloped in mist and idle chatter, the reciters of hymns wander about, seeking only their own sustenance.
O Manyu, wielder of the thunderbolt and arrow, he who honors you nourishes all-encompassing power and strength continuously.
With you as our ally—born of strength, powerful through your might—may we overcome both the Dāsa and the Ārya.
Manyu is Indra; Manyu indeed was the god; Manyu is the Hotṛ, Varuṇa, and Jātavedas.
The human tribes that exist offer praise to Manyu; O Manyu, protect us, being in harmony with your fervor.
Come hither, O Manyu, you who are more powerful than the powerful; with heat as your ally, strike down our enemies.
As the slayer of foes, the slayer of Vṛtra, and the slayer of Dasyus, bring all riches unto us.
For you, O Manyu, possess overwhelming power; you are self-existent, radiant, and the subduer of adversaries.
O Manyu, who art the lord of all people, victorious and triumphant, bestow upon us strength in battles.
Being without a share, O wise one, I have gone away from you, though you are powerful by your own will.
I, lacking in resolve, have provoked your anger; come to me, O Manyu, as your own body, to grant me strength.
I am here for you; come toward me, O Conqueror, facing this way, you who provide all sustenance.
O Manyu, wielder of the thunderbolt, turn toward me; let us two slay the Dasyus, and may you be mindful of our work.
Come forward, be at my right hand, and then let us strike down the many Vṛtras.
RV 10.83.7.2: I offer to you the sustaining first portion of the honeyed [soma]; let us both drink the *upāṃśu* draught first.

RV 10.84.1.1: With you, O Manyu, riding on the same chariot, breaking through [the enemy], exulting, bold, and accompanied by the Maruts— RV 10.84.1.2: Men with sharp arrows, whetting their weapons, possessing the form of fire, let them advance.
Like Agni, O Manyu, blazing with brilliance, be our victorious leader, O Conqueror, when invoked!
Having slain the enemies, distribute their wealth; measuring out your power, drive away those who oppose us.
Overpower, O Manyu, the one who assails us; breaking, crushing, and utterly destroying, go forth against the enemies!
Your fierce might has indeed been checked; as the subduer, you alone bring them under your control, O sole-born one.
You alone are the wrathful one among the many; sharpen every clan for battle.
With you as our ally, we—whose splendor is unimpaired—raise a brilliant shout for victory.
Like Indra, the maker of victory, who is never held back, O Manyu, be our protector here.
We celebrate your beloved name, O Conqueror; we know that spring from which you have arisen.
With your innate power, O wielder of the thunderbolt and the arrow, you bear superior conquering might, O Overcomer.
O Manyu, through our wisdom, be with us in the encounter for great wealth, O you who are invoked by many!
May both kinds of gathered wealth, brought together, be granted to us by Varuṇa and Manyu.
Let the enemies, placing fear in their hearts, being utterly defeated, sink away into concealment. By Truth is the earth supported; by the Sun is the sky supported.
By Cosmic Order (*ṛta*) the Ādityas stand firm; Soma is established in heaven.
Through Soma the Ādityas are strong; through Soma the earth is great.
Thus, in the lap of these stars, Soma is established.
One thinks he has drunk Soma when they grind the plant.
That Soma which the Brahmins know—no one at all eats of it.
Guarded by various arrangements, O Soma, you are protected by the Bṛhatī verses;
Standing there, you listen to the pressing-stones; no earthly being eats of you.
When they drink you, O God, from there you swell again;
Vāyu is the protector of Soma, and the month is the form of the year. Raibhī was the follower, Nārāśaṃsī the one who settled down.
For Sūryā, a beautiful garment, adorned with song, was brought;
thought was her pillow, sight her ointment.
Heaven and earth were her bridal chest when Sūryā went to her husband.
The hymns were the cross-bars; the *kurira* was the head-ornament; the *chandas* was the crest-ornament.
The Aśvins were the suitors for Sūryā; Agni was the leader of the procession.
Soma became the bridegroom; both the Aśvins were the suitors.
Savitṛ gave Sūryā to her husband as she was praising him with her mind.
The mind was her vehicle; the sky was her canopy.
The two bright ones were her draft-oxen when Sūryā went to the great [wedding].
Your two oxen are impelled by the *Ṛk* and *Sāman*; they are covered with the *Sāman*.
Your two ears were the wheels; your path was in heaven, moving to and fro.
Your two wheels are pure as you go; the *Vyāna* breath is the axle that has been set in place.
Sūryā ascended the incomparable chariot, setting out for her husband.
The bridal procession of Sūryā has gone forth, which Savitṛ sent away.
The cattle of the two Arjunīs are slain; she is being carried around.
When you two, O Aśvins, were asked and came as the bridal procession for Sūryā on your three-wheeled chariot, all the gods recognized that deed of yours; Pūṣan, the son, chose you as his parents.
When you went, O Lords of Splendor, to choose Sūryā as your bride.
Where was your single wheel? Where did you stand for the sake of the commander?
O Sūryā, two wheels of yours the Brahmans know according to the seasons;
but that one wheel which is hidden, only those who possess true knowledge know it.
To Sūryā, to the gods, to Mitra and Varuṇa— to those who are the wise overseers of all that has come to be—to them I have paid this homage.
These two move one after the other by means of their creative power (*māyā*); like two children at play, they go around the sacrifice.
One of them surveys all beings; the other, ordaining the seasons, is born again.
Being born, he becomes ever new; as the banner of the days, he goes at the head of the dawns.
Coming forth, he distributes his portion to the gods; the moon extends his long life-span.

Mount this chariot of the immortal world, O Sūryā—made of fine *kiṃśuka* wood, of *śalmali*, multiform, golden-hued, well-rolling, and with excellent wheels. Make the journey pleasant for your husband.
Arise from here, for you are now possessed of a husband! I honor Viśvāvasu with reverence and with songs of praise.
Seek another who sits among the Fathers; she is manifest. Know that she is your portion by birth.
Rise up from here, O Viśvāvasu; I bow before you with praise, for you are great.
Seek another who is vigorous; unite her as a wife with her husband.
May the paths be thornless and straight by which our friends go; may we go forward.
May Aryaman lead us together, may Bhaga lead us together; O Gods, may our lordship be well-governed.
I release you from the bond of Varuṇa, with which Savitṛ, the very gracious, bound you.
In the womb of Truth, in the world of the well-performed deed, I place you, unharmed, together with your husband.
I release her from here, not from there; I have made her well-bound from that side.
O bounteous Indra, so that she may be rich in sons and fortunate.
May Pūṣan lead you from here, taking your hand; may the Aśvins carry you away on their chariot.
Go to the house so that you may be the mistress of the household; as one who has power, may you speak at the assembly.
May what is dear to you be fulfilled here through offspring; in this house, as the mistress of the home, remain ever watchful.
With this husband, unite your body; then, growing old together, you two shall speak at the assembly.
It becomes blue and red; the attachment of the sorcery is revealed. His kinsmen prosper; the husband is bound in bonds.
Give away the woolen garment; distribute wealth among the Brahmins.
This woman has become a sorceress, a bringer of misfortune; as a wife, she enters her husband.
Her body becomes unlovely and pale through that wickedness.
When the husband seeks to cover his own limb with the garment of his bride;
when the consumption-diseases that follow the bride’s bright bridal procession from among the people—
may the worshipful gods lead them back again to the place from which they came.
May the highwaymen who lie in wait not find the couple; having passed through the difficult path by easy ways, let the enemies flee away.
This bride is most auspicious; come together and behold her.
Having bestowed good fortune upon her, depart now and go back to your homes.
This is harsh, this is bitter; like a bone with a splinter, it is like poison—it is not to be eaten.
Only that Brahmin who knows Sūryā deserves the bride-price.
The carving, the cutting up, and then the slicing—Sūryā, behold these forms; the Brahman purifies them.
I take your hand for the sake of good fortune, so that you may reach old age with me as your husband.
Bhaga, Aryaman, Savitṛ, and Purandhi—the gods have given you to me for the office of householder.
O Pūṣan, impel her toward us as most auspicious, she in whom men sow the seed;
she who, longing, spreads apart her thighs for us, and in whom we, longing, shall cast our member.
For you, O Agni, they first drove Sūryā around with her bridal procession; give back the wife to her husbands along with offspring.
Agni has given back the wife with long life and with splendor.
May he who is her husband live a long life for a hundred autumns. Soma first obtained her; Gandharva obtained her next.
Agni was your third husband; your fourth is born of man.
Soma gave [her] to the Gandharva; the Gandharva gave [her] to Agni.
And Agni has given me wealth and sons, as well as this woman. Stay right here; do not be parted; enjoy the full span of life.
Playing with sons and grandsons, rejoicing in your own home—may Prajāpati grant us offspring; may Aryaman anoint us for long life.
Enter the world of your husband, O you of auspicious fortune! Be a blessing to our bipeds and a blessing to our quadrupeds.
With eyes that are not terrible, do not be a slayer of your husband; be auspicious toward our cattle, well-disposed, and full of luster.
May you be a mother of heroes, loving the gods, and pleasant; be a source of blessing to us, to our bipeds, and to our quadrupeds.
O bounteous Indra, make this woman rich in sons and fortunate.
Bestow upon her ten sons; make her husband the eleventh. Be a sovereign queen over your father-in-law;
be a sovereign queen over your mother-in-law. Be a sovereign queen over your sister-in-law;
be a sovereign queen over your brothers-in-law.
May all the gods unite our hearts; may the waters unite them.
May Mātariśvan unite them, may Dhātṛ unite them, and may the Goddess of Direction unite us both.
For they have flowed away from the presser; they did not honor Indra as a god.
Where the bull Vṛṣākapi has rejoiced, my friend among the prosperous ones—Indra is superior to all.
O Indra, you run far away from Vṛṣākapi’s distress; you do not find us anywhere else for the drinking of Soma—Indra is superior to all.
What has this Vṛṣākapi done to you, this tawny beast, that you now desire him? Whether it be wealth or nourishment, O Indra, you are superior to all.
[This is] the Vṛṣākapi whom you, O Indra, protect as a dear friend.
May the dog indeed gnaw at his ear, even as he seeks to strike; Indra is superior to all.
The monkey has spoiled for me those dear, well-fashioned, and polished things.
May I rend his head; may I not be an easy path for the evildoer. Indra is superior to all.
No woman has been better at the loom than I, nor more skillful at the shuttle; no one has drawn the shuttles closer together, nor raised the thighs higher. Indra is superior to all.
O Mother, O easy-to-find one! Indeed, as it shall be, so shall it be.
My buttocks itch, my thighs itch, and my head seems to tingle; Indra is superior to all.
(RV 10.86.7) O fair-armed one, O lovely-fingered, broad-chested, broad-hipped woman! Why do you, as the wife of a hero, revile Vṛṣākapi? Indra is superior to all. (RV 10.86.8)
This hunter regards me as if I were childless;
yet I am indeed possessed of sons, the wife of Indra, and have the Maruts as my friends. Indra is superior to all.
Long ago, a woman used to go to the common sacrifice or the assembly.
The wife of Indra, the creator of the cosmic order, the mother of heroes, is magnified; Indra is superior to all.
Among these women, I have heard that Indrāṇī is most fortunate;
for her husband shall never die of old age hereafter. Indra is superior to all.
O Indrāṇī, I have no pleasure except for my friend Vṛṣākapi, whose beloved oblation, consisting of water, goes to the gods; Indra is superior to all.
O wealthy Vṛṣākapāyī, you who have a good son and a good daughter-in-law!
RV 10.86.13: O Indra, you shall eat my oxen, the dear oblation that brings fulfillment; O Indra, you are higher than all. RV 10.86.14: For fifteen oxen they cook for me at once, even twenty;
and I eat the fatness; both my flanks fill me full; O Indra, you are higher than all.
Like a bull with sharp horns bellowing amidst the herds, O Indra, the stirred drink is a joy to the heart for you who press it out with devotion; O Indra, you are superior to all.
He does not master that which dangles between his thighs, the [sacrificial] ladle.
He whose hairy member, when he sits down, expands—Indra is superior to all.
No one is master of him whose hairy member, when he sits down, expands.
He whose member dangles between his thighs like a wooden pin—Indra is superior to all.
O Indra, this Vṛṣākapi has found a slain wild beast;
he has discovered a fresh porridge of entrails piled up at the place of wood-fuel. O Indra, you are superior to all.
I go here, looking out and discerning between the Dāsa and the Ārya.
Let me drink, O you who have pressed the Soma; I have looked toward the wise one. Indra is superior to all.
The desert and the place of carving—how many *yojanas* apart are they?
O Vṛṣākapi, come closer; go home. Indra is superior to all.
Return, O Vṛṣākapi; let us two arrange our well-being.
You who go to sleep, you who travel along the paths, you, O Indra, are higher than all. When you, O Vṛṣākapi, went home toward the north, O Indra—
Where is that beast of many sins? To whom has he gone, the one who brings trouble to men? Indra is superior to all.
She who was named Parśu, the daughter of Manu, gave birth at once to twenty children.
It was a blessing for her; it was a good thing for her whose womb was diseased. Indra is superior to all.
I anoint the slayer of demons, the vigorous one; I approach the most extensive Mitra for protection.
May Agni, sharpened by our rites and kindled, protect us from harm by day and by night.
O Jātavedas, kindled with your flame, touch the sorcerers with your iron teeth.
Seize the false gods with your tongue; having torn apart the flesh-eaters, place them within your jaws.
Set both sets of tusks, one above and one below, sharpening yourself as a predator. O King, roam through the mid-air and strike the sorcerers with your jaws.
O Agni, fashioning arrows with sacrifices and sharpening their points with speech like thunderbolts— with these, pierce the sorcerers in the heart; break their arms as they turn toward you.
O Agni, split open the skin of the sorcerer; let the destructive thunderbolt strike him down with its heat.
O Jātavedas, rend his joints asunder; let the flesh-eater, craving raw flesh, tear apart what is mangled.
O Agni Jātavedas, wherever you now see him—whether he is standing still or moving about, or whether he is flying through the paths of the mid-air—pierce him with your arrow, whetting it keenly.
And seize him who has not yet been caught, O Jātavedas; from the sorcerer (*yātudhāna*) who has seized us, strike him down with your spears.
O Agni, blazing forth, strike him down first; let the raw-flesh-eating, dark-colored vultures devour him.
Speak here, O Agni, which one it is—the sorcerer who does this.
Seize him with your fuel, O youngest one; subject him to the eye of the one who beholds men.
With your sharp eye, O Agni, protect the sacrifice; lead it forward toward the Vasus, O wise one.
Let not the sorcerers harm you as you blaze against the injurious demons, O beholder of men.
O watcher of men, look out for the *rakṣas* among the people; crush his three foremost parts.
O Agni, crush his ribs with your heat; tear up the root of the sorcerer in three ways.
Let the sorcerer’s snare pass him by thrice, he who strikes the truth, O Agni, with falsehood.
O Jātavedas, flashing forth with your radiance, overcome this man in the very presence of the one who praises you.
O Agni, bestow upon the singer that eye wherewith you behold the hoof-striking sorcerer. Like Atharvan, consume with divine light the faithless one who injures the truth.

O Agni, whatever curse a pair utters today, or whatever harshness of speech the people produce among themselves—whatever arrow is born from the mind and the thought—with that, pierce the sorcerers in their hearts.
Strike down the sorcerers with your heat; O Agni, strike down the *rakṣas* with your flame.
With your flame, crush the fools who worship false gods; burning fiercely, destroy those who delight in the breath of others.
May the gods today crush the wicked man;
may harsh curses return upon him. May arrows strike the thief in his vital organs; let the sorcerer fall into the snare of everyone.
The sorcerer who anoints himself with human flesh, or with the flesh of a horse,
or who steals the milk of the cow— O Agni, strike off their heads with your fiery heat!
O you who watch over men, let not the sorcerer consume the yearly milk of the cow!
O Agni, whatever nectar the sorcerers (*yātudhāna*) seek to devour, pierce him from behind with your flame at his vital spot.
Let the sorcerers drink the poison of the cows; let the wicked ones be cut off from Aditi’s wide space.
May the god Savitṛ deliver them over; may they lose their share of the plants and perish.
From of old, O Agni, you have crushed the sorcerers; the *rakṣas* demons have not overcome you in battle.
Burn up the flesh-eaters along with their roots; let none escape your divine weapon.
O Agni, protect us from below and from above; protect us from behind and from the front.
May those unaging, most fervent flames of thine consume the one who utters evil against us.
O King, as a seer, protect us from behind, from before, from below, and from above through thy wisdom. O Agni, immortal friend, do thou, the ageless, lead us mortals to old age.
O Agni, O powerful one, we place you around us as a fortress— you, the inspired sage, of bold appearance, day by day the slayer of those who deal treacherously.
With your poison, burn up the treacherous ones and the demons.
O Agni, with your sharp flame and with your spears tipped with fire, O Agni,
burn against the pairs of Yātudhānas and Kimīdins.
I sharpen you, O inspired one, like a blade, so that you may grow strong and remain inviolate through my prayers.
O Agni, with your heat, crush the heat [of the enemy] on every side;
shatter the strength and the heroic power of the *yātudhāna* and the *rakṣas*.
The oblation, which is ageless, a protector, and found in the light, is offered into Agni—the one who touches the heavens—as a welcome gift.
For his support, for the sake of the world, the gods spread themselves out by their own inherent power for the sake of the cosmic order.
When Agni was born, the swallowed world, hidden in darkness, became manifest, and the light appeared.
The gods—the earth, the sky, and the waters—delighted in his friendship, as did the plants.
Sent forth by the gods worthy of sacrifice, I shall praise Agni, the ageless and great one,
who with his radiance has stretched across this earth and heaven, and the two worlds, the mid-air;
he who was the first invoker beloved by the gods, whom they chose while anointing him with clarified butter.
He made the world that was moving with wings subject to his own power; Agni Jātavedas performed this deed.

O Agni Jātavedas, since you stood upon the summit of the universe together with the realm of light, we approach you with our thoughts, songs, and hymns; thus you became worthy of sacrifice, filling both heaven and earth.
Agni becomes the head of the world by night; from him the sun is born as it rises in the morning.
Among those worthy of sacrifice, he moves swiftly through the waters, knowing them well.
He who, kindled in his greatness, is beautiful to behold, has shone forth with radiant light, having heaven as his birthplace.
In that fire, all the gods who protect their own bodies offered oblations with the *sūktavāka*. First, the gods generated the *sūktavāka* from Agni; first they generated the oblation from Agni.
That [Agni] became their sacrifice, the protector of their bodies; him Heaven knew, him Earth, and him the Waters.
The gods who generated this Agni, in whom they offered up all the worlds— he, straightening himself,
heated the earth and this heaven with his flame through his greatness. For by means of praise, the gods generated Agni in heaven with their powers, he who fills both worlds.
They made him threefold for the sake of existence; he ripens the plants of every form.
When the worshipful gods placed Sūrya, the son of Aditi, in heaven, then that the two moving pairs became manifest, all living beings beheld them.
The gods have made Agni Vaiśvānara the banner for the entire world and for the days;
he who has spread out the shining dawns and uncovers the waters by covering over the darkness with his flame.
The wise, worshipful gods generated Agni Vaiśvānara, the ageless one.
We address with hymns Agni the Seer, the ancient star that moves, the overseer of the spirit, the powerful and vast Vaiśvānara who shines forever,
who by his greatness has encompassed the two wide worlds, the god who is both here below and beyond.
I have heard of two paths of the fathers and of the gods, as well as of mortals.
Along these two, all this moving world comes together—that which lies between the father and the mother. The two united ones bear him who moves about, born from the head, fashioned by the mind.
He stands facing all beings, unwearied, the swift one, shining brightly.
Where the lower and the higher speak together, which of us two, the two sacrificers, knows [the truth]?
The friends have reached the common feast; they have attained the sacrifice—who will proclaim this?
How many are the fires? How many are the suns? How many are the dawns? And how many indeed are the waters?
O Fathers, I do not speak to you in jest; I ask you, O sages, for the sake of knowledge.
As great as is the face of the Dawn, so do the well-winged ones dwell within Mātariśvan.
So much does the Brahmin bestow as he approaches the sacrifice, sitting down below the Hotṛ-priest.
Praise Indra, the most heroic, by whose greatness the luminous realms and the ends of the earth were forced apart;
he who, upholding the people with his strengths, has surpassed the rivers in his majesty.
May he, Indra, turn the sun around the wide spaces like the wheels of a chariot;
he struck down the black darkness with his splendor, like a flood that does not stand still.
Sing for him a common, never-ceasing song—new prayer, peerless, from the earth and from heaven.
He who, like a king, has surveyed all births as if they were his own backs—Indra, our friend, seeks his companion.
For Indra, I have sent forth songs with unrestrained flow, like waters released from the depths of the ocean;
he who, by his powers, has propped apart the earth and heaven on all sides, as if with two wheels held by an axle.
With his fury stirred, impetuous in onset, roaring, powerful, armed with the *śaru* weapon, and drinking the dregs—Soma overcomes all forests on this side; no counter-measures have deceived Indra.
Neither heaven and earth, nor the desert, nor the mid-air, nor the mountains have contained Soma when he flowed forth.
When his wrath is directed against him, he rends the firm and breaks down even the strong;
he struck down Vṛtra as an axe fells trees, he shattered the fortresses and dug out the rivers for us. He split the mountain like a new jar; Indra brought forth the cows with his own companions.
O Indra, wise one, you indeed cut through that debt like a sharp sword; you shatter the crooked ones as if they were joints of wood.
Those men who violate the law of Mitra and Varuṇa, as if destroying a close ally—those evildoers who transgress against Mitra, Aryaman, the *saṃgir* (the covenant), and Varuṇa.
O Indra, O bull, sharpen your mighty, ruddy, and bull-like weapon against the enemies.
Indra rules over heaven; Indra rules over the earth; Indra rules over the waters; Indra indeed rules over the mountains.
Indra is the strengthener of the great; Indra is the lord of the wise; Indra is to be invoked in times of peace and in times of exertion.
Indra has surpassed you, O Vṛtra, from the days that have passed, from the mid-air, and from the depth of the ocean.
He has surpassed the expanse of the wind, the ends of the earth, the rivers, and all inhabited lands.
Like the gleaming banner of the dawning dawn, let your insatiable bolt, O Indra, roll forth.
Like a stone, pierce through from heaven, releasing them with your most scorching heat; strike down the deceitful enemies.
Day after day, month after month, the forests, the plants, and the mountains followed him.
Both worlds, crying out in longing, and the waters followed Indra as he was being born.
When indeed, O Indra, was that deed of yours known, when you shattered the devouring demon?
When those who betray their friends lay scattered upon the earth like cattle in a slaughterhouse, fleeing in terror?
O Indra, those who sought to harm us have risen up against us; they swell with great pride as a host of aggressors.
May the enemies be overtaken by blinding darkness; may the nights be full of light for them.
For many are the libations of men that have gladdened you, and the prayers of the chanting seers. Hearing this invocation with favor, come hither across all those who sing your praises.
RV_10.089.17.1 Thus may we, O Indra, enjoy your ever-new and gracious favors.
RV_10.089.17.2 May we, the Viśvāmitras, singing your praises, find your protection at the break of dawn, even now, O Indra.
RV_10.089.18.1 We invoke for our welfare the generous Maghavan...
The Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet. Having pervaded the earth on all sides, he stands beyond it by the measure of ten fingers.
This Puruṣa alone is all this—whatever has been and whatever is yet to be.
And he is the lord of immortality, that which grows by means of food.
Such is his greatness, and yet the Puruṣa is even greater than this. All beings constitute one quarter of him; his three quarters are the immortal in heaven.
The Puruṣa rose up, three-quarters of him being above; one-quarter of him remained here below. From there he strode out in all directions, pervading both that which eats and that which does not eat.
From him Virāj was born; from Virāj, the Puruṣa was born.
Once born, he extended beyond the earth behind and before.
When the gods performed the sacrifice with the Puruṣa as the oblation,
Spring was its clarified butter, Summer the fuel, and Autumn the offering.
They sprinkled that sacrifice, the Puruṣa born in the beginning, upon the sacrificial grass;
with him the gods, the Sādhyas, and the Ṛṣis sacrificed.
From that sacrifice, in which everything was offered, the speckled butter was gathered.

He created those animals belonging to Vāyu—both those of the forest and those of the village—from that sacrifice in which everything was offered. From that sacrifice the *ṛc*s and the *sāman*s were born;
from it the meters were born, and from it the *yajus* was produced.
From him were born horses, and whatever animals have two rows of teeth;
from him cows were produced, and from him goats and sheep were born.
When they divided the Puruṣa, into how many parts did they arrange him?
"What was his mouth? What were his two arms? What were called his thighs and feet?
"The Brāhmaṇa was his mouth; his two arms were made into the Rājanya (Kṣatriya);
his thighs were the Vaiśya; from his feet the Śūdra was born."
From his mind the moon was born; from his eye the sun was born. From his mouth Indra and Agni were born; from his breath Vāyu was born.
From his navel the intermediate space arose; from his head the sky evolved.
From his feet they fashioned the earth, and from his hearing the quarters; thus they formed the worlds.
Seven were his enclosing sticks, and thrice seven were made the fuel-sticks, when the gods, performing the sacrifice, bound Puruṣa as the victim.
By means of sacrifice the gods sacrificed to the Sacrifice; those were the first established laws (*dharmāṇi*).

These great ones attained the firmament (*nākam*), where the ancient *Sādhyas*, the gods, abide. The domestic lord (*damūnāḥ*), being praised by the watchful ones, is kindled in the house at the place of the dwelling, providing nourishment.
The Hotṛ-priest of every oblation, most desirable, pervasive and radiant, he is a true friend to him who seeks his friendship.
He, of beautiful splendor, dwells as a guest in every house, taking refuge in every forest like a bird of swift flight.
Belonging to all people, he does not despise any person; as one of the people, he dwells among the clans, visiting every clan.

O Agni, you are most skillful through your skills, and by your wisdom you are most wise; you are a seer through your seerhood, the knower of all. As the Vasu among treasures, you alone rule over all wealth; both Heaven and Earth cause it to prosper.
Knowing it well, O Agni, you have sat down upon your seasonal birthplace, rich in ghee, at the station of Iḷā.
Thy arrivals are as wondrous as those of the dawns, like the stainless rays of the sun.
Thy glories are as brilliant as the lightnings of the rain-cloud; they shine forth like the banners of the dawns.
When thou art let loose upon the plants and the forests, thou gatherest for thyself food from all sides into thy mouth.
The plants received him as their timely germ; the waters, the mothers, brought forth him, Agni.
Him, the same one, the trees and the creepers bring forth continually, and those who are pregnant give birth to him.
When fanned by the wind and impelled according to your wills, you spread abroad, swiftly consuming the food.

RV 10.91.7: Your undecaying flames, O Agni, as you burn, spread out separately like chariot-horses. RV 10.91.8: Agni, the maker of wisdom, the accomplisher of the sacrifice, the invoker, the most pervasive thought—him indeed they choose for the small oblation and him equally for the great; none other than you.

RV 10.91.9: Here, O Agni, the wise ones who desire you choose you as the Hotṛ-priest in the sacrificial assemblies, when the god-seeking men, possessing oblations and having trimmed the sacred grass, present their offerings to you.

RV 10.91.10: Yours, O Agni, is the office of the Hotṛ; yours is the office of the Potṛ at the appointed time; yours is the office of the Neṣṭṛ; you are the Agnidh for him who follows the cosmic order.
Thou art the *praśāstṛ*, thou officiatest as the *adhvaryu*, thou art the *brahmán* and the master of the house within our home.
O Agni, whatever mortal offers to thee, the immortal, with fuel or prepares an oblation— for him thou actest as the *hotṛ*;
thou goest on thy mission as messenger; thou speakest for him, thou sacrificest, and thou officiatest as the *adhvaryu*.
These thoughts, these words from us, these verses, songs, and well-spoken hymns have come together for him.
Seeking wealth, he has taken pleasure in these increasing prayers for the sake of the wealthy Jātavedas, even though they were already great.
May I utter this newest, well-spoken hymn for the ancient one who desires it; may he hear us.
May she be within his heart to touch it, like a loving, well-dressed wife for her husband. In whom horses, bulls, oxen, barren cows, and rams are set loose and offered as oblations—
To that Agni, the drinker of sweet draughts, whose back is laden with Soma, the ordainer, I generate a beautiful hymn from my heart.
The oblation has been poured into your mouth, O Agni, like ghee into the ladle, like Soma into the cup.
Bestow upon us wealth that wins booty, rich in heroes, highly praised, glorious, and vast.
I praise you, the charioteer of the sacrifice, the lord of the people, the invoker of the clans, the guest of the night, the one rich in light.
Flaming among the dry shrubs and flickering among the green ones, the bull, the holy banner, has ascended to heaven.
Both gods and men have made this Agni their easy-to-approach upholder of the law, the accomplisher of the sacrifice.
Like the young sun, they kiss the Dawn’s high priest, Tanūnapāt, the ruddy one.
We discern his paths and the thoughts of the Paṇi; his branches were offered for him to consume. When the terrible ones attained immortality, they then celebrated the divine race of men.
For the bond of *ṛta* is heaven, wide-extending; homage is great, and the spirit of devotion is most excellent.
Indra, Mitra, and Varuṇa have come together in harmony; so too Bhaga and Savitṛ, whose will is pure.
With the swiftly-moving Rudra, the rivers flow forth; they have rushed across the great earth, beyond all weariness.
By them, as the wanderer traverses the wide expanse, he roars aloud and sprinkles everything within his belly.
The active Rudras and Maruts, who belong to all tribes, are the falcons of heaven, the dwellers in the home of the Asura.
With them—Varuṇa, Mitra, Aryaman, and Indra—shines the swift one together with the swift gods.
In Indra have those who toil found enjoyment, in the sight of the Sun and in the manly power of the Bull.

The poets who have fashioned for themselves a claim to his honor, and have forged the companion thunderbolt for the assemblies of men— even the sun has stayed his bay horses; everyone fears Indra, for he is more powerful than any other.
From the belly of the terrifying bull, as he breathes forth, the one who brings wealth thunders day after day, unoppressed.
Today, with homage, offer a hymn of praise to your skillful Rudra, the ruler of heroes— those auspicious ones who,
swift-moving and self-glorious, accompany him from heaven with their eager steeds. For they, Bṛhaspati the bull and the kinsmen of Soma, have spread wide renown among their progeny.
Through sacrifices, Atharvan first established the order; through skillful powers, the Bhṛgus became fully conscious of the gods.
For they—Heaven and Earth, who possess abundant seed, Narāśaṃsa, Caturaṅga, Yama, Aditi, the god Tvaṣṭṛ, Draviṇodās, the Ṛbhukṣans, Rodasī, the Maruts, and Viṣṇu—have vied for preeminence.
And may that inspired sage, Ahi Budhnya, hear our call from afar; may he, the seer, listen to us who yearn for him.
May Sūrya and Māsā, who move apart and dwell in heaven, and Dhiyāśams and Huṣī, take notice of this prayer of his.
May Pūṣan, who belongs to all the gods, and Apāṃ Napāt, and Vāyu, further our journey for the sake of our well-being.
Sing forth to the Wind for our greater welfare; O Aśvins, easily invoked, hear this on your journey!
We praise with songs him who dwells above these fearless tribes, the self-glorious one.
With all the divine dames, we celebrate Aditi, the peerless, and the youthful lord of the night, whose mind is set on manly deeds.
RV 10.92.15: Here, by his very birth, the ancient Aṅgiras sang; the pressing-stones, looking upward, beheld the sacrifice.
By means of these, the far-seeing one became expansive; the well-established path was like an axe in a forest.
RV 10.93.1: O Heaven and Earth, become great and wide for us; like two young women, like two vast worlds, be our seat.
With these, protect us in our struggle; with these, protect us in our exertion.
At every sacrifice, that mortal honors the gods—whoever, being most renowned for his renown, seeks to win them over with propitious hymns.
They are the sovereign rulers of all the gods, possessing great majesty. All of them are truly all-pervading in their greatness; all are worthy of sacrifice at the rituals.
They indeed are the joyful kings of immortality: Aryaman, Mitra, Varuṇa, and Parijman.
When is Rudra praised among men? O Maruts, Pūṣan, and Bhaga!
And may Sūryā and Māsa, the lords of wealth, come to our dwelling at night with the waters, together with that which belongs to the Dragon of the Deep in the depths.
And may the two gods, the Aśvins, lords of splendor, and Mitrāvaruṇa protect us with their powers.
He hastens toward great wealth, overcoming difficulties as if crossing a desert.
And may even the Rudras be gracious to us, the Aśvins, all the gods, Rathaspati, and Bhaga.
R̥bhu, Vāja, and R̥bhukṣan, you who travel all around, possessors of all wealth!

R̥bhu, R̥bhukṣan, and R̥bhu—your exhilaration comes from the worshiper; may your two bay steeds, swift and vigorous, hasten toward you, you whose Sāman is difficult to surpass, and whose human sacrifice is performed with perfect success.
O God Savitṛ, make us free from shame; may he be praised among the wealthy patrons.
Like Indra with his steeds, he has drawn forth the wheel and the reins of these people.
O Heaven and Earth, bestow upon these our heroes great and all-encompassing fame.
For the winning of strength, for the gaining of wealth, [we seek] nourishment.
O Indra, you who are well-disposed toward us, wherever this singer may be, O powerful one, always protect him for our aid—for our aid.
May he prosper, O Vasu, through his knowledge.
They have increased this hymn of mine, which has a radiant course like the sun, as the patrons have increased it;
like a carpenter fashioning a horse-harness that does not fall apart, they have made it firm.
Their golden chariot, yoked with wealth, has turned toward us.
Their manly deeds were like those of archers at the mark; their ends were reached as if in sport.
I have proclaimed this before Duḥśīma, Pṛthavāna, Vena, Rāma, and the Asuras and Maghavans— those who, having yoked five hundred [horses], have made their path resound for us.
RV 10.93.15: Here, indeed, he has bestowed seventy-seven [cows] upon us;
Tānva has bestowed them instantly, Pārthya has bestowed them instantly, and Māyava has bestowed them instantly.
RV 10.94.1: Let these speak forth, let us speak forth; utter the word to the stones that have already spoken!
When you, O pressing-stones, swift as mountains, together bring forth the song and the sound for Indra, O possessors of Soma;
these stones speak out with a hundredfold and thousandfold voice, they roar aloud with their golden jaws.
Having performed their work well through their skillful action, the stones, as the first, have attained the right to eat the oblation even before the Hotṛ-priest.
These ones speak, having found the honey; they chant the *nyūṅkha* over the cooked meat. Chewing upon the branch of the ruddy tree, those well-fed bulls have bellowed forth.
They speak loudly with the exhilarating, intoxicating drink, calling out to Indra, having found the honey.
Exhilarated, the wise ones have danced with their sisters, making the earth resound with their rhythmic footsteps.
Like well-winged birds, they have raised their voices toward the sky; the dark, impetuous ones have danced upon the mountain ridges.
They descend to the appointed place of the lower region; shining like the sun, they have deposited abundant seed.
Like fierce ones rushing forward, they have come together; yoked at once, the two bulls bear the poles. When they pant and swallow, they roar; one hears their snorting like that of racing steeds.
[I praise] them who have ten fingers, ten girths, ten yokes, and ten traces.

Let us sing praise to the ten reins that do not grow old, to the ten poles, and to the ten yoked ones that carry the burden. These stones have ten mechanisms and are swift; their setting in place is a desirable thing to behold.
They have partaken of the first nectar of the stalk, of the pressed Soma juice.
Those Soma-drinkers kiss the two bay steeds of Indra; milking the stalk, they sit upon the cow.
Having drunk the Soma-mead milked by them, Indra grows strong, spreads abroad, and acts as a bull.
Your stalk is indeed a bull; you have never been harmed. You always remain full of sap, well-fed.
Like the wealth of Raivata, you are beautiful in your greatness, O stones, you whom we have delighted in this sacrifice.
The stones are porous yet not porous, unexhausted, unfettered, and immortal;
they are free from disease, ageless, steadfast, well-fleshed, without thirst, and free from craving.
O Fathers, firm indeed are you from age to age; desiring security, they do not leave their seat.
Undecaying, following the golden path, with golden speed, they have made heaven and earth resound with their roar.
At the unyoking, the pressing-stones speak thus at the journey’s end, as if with the distinct sounds of hooves.

Like grain-gatherers sowing seed, they mix the Soma; devouring it, they do not diminish it. At the pressed sacrifice, they have raised their voices, like playful children pricking their mother. Release well the inspired thought of the one who has pressed [the juice]; let the pressing-stones roll away as they are being honored.
Come, O wife! Stay with me in spirit, O terrible one; let us now exchange words together.
These unspoken counsels of ours shall bring us no joy, even on a future day.
What shall I do with these words of yours? I have already set forth, like the first light of the dawn.
O Purūravas, return again to your home; I am as difficult to capture as the wind.
Like an arrow from a quiver, like the beauty of a bowstring, I am a winner of cattle, a swift racer winning hundreds.
When the will is without a hero, they flash like lightning; like lowing cows, the impetuous ones have made me conscious.
Bestowing wealth upon her father-in-law, O Dawn, when she desired to go from her husband's house, she reached the home of him in whom she delighted—
him who pierced her day and night with his reed-staff. Three times a day you have pierced me with your reed-staff, and yet you have not filled me, even though you were close at hand.
O Purūravas, I have come according to your desire; O hero, you were the king of my body.

She who is well-kindled, a row [of flames], a kinswoman of bliss, who gazes into the heart like an eye, moving about like one who unties a knot— those ointments have flowed forth like ruddy [dawns]; for the sake of glory, they have lowed like milch-cows.
When he was born, the divine dames sat together, and the self-praising rivers increased him.
O Purūravas, when the gods strengthened you for the great battle, for the slaying of the Dasyus.
When, as a mortal, I dwelt among those non-human women who had cast aside their human garment.
Like a woman longing for her lover, they have hastened away; like horses touching the chariot, they were terrified.
When the mortal man has touched these immortal ones, he unites with them as with the worlds through his mental powers.
Like birds, they adorn their own bodies; like playful horses, they bite and paw the ground.
Like a flashing lightning bolt falling with a roar, she brought to me the desirable waters of the deep.
The hero among men was born from the waters, well-born; may Urvaśī prolong her long life.
You were indeed born for the protection of the cattle; you have bestowed that power upon us, O Purūravas.
I, who know, instructed you on that very day; yet you did not listen to me—what do you say now, you who have failed to enjoy?
When will the son, once born, desire his father? When, perceiving it, will he shed tears?
Who shall separate the husband and wife who are of one mind, while the fire shines among the parents-in-law?
I shall answer back to him who sheds tears; he shall not cry out like one who weeps for his beloved.
I will send forth that which is yours among us; go home, O simple-minded one, do not follow after us.
May the virtuous man fly away today, never to return, to go to the furthest distance.
Then he shall lie in the lap of Nirṛti, and there the impetuous wolves shall devour him.
O Purūravas, do not die, do not perish; let not the malevolent wolves devour you.
There are no friendships with women; these are but the hearts of hyenas.
When I, Virūpa, dwelt among mortals for four autumn nights, I ate a single drop of clarified butter once a day; with that alone I move about, fully satisfied even now.
Vasiṣṭha pays homage to Urvaśī, who fills the mid-air and measures out the region of space.
May the gift of your good deed attend you; turn back, for my heart is burning with grief.
Thus do these gods say to you, O Iḷā: "Since you have thus become a kinsman of death, let your offspring worship the gods with oblations, and you too shall rejoice in heaven."
I shall proclaim your two bay steeds at the great assembly; I win for you the desirable exhilaration from the one who desires it.
He who pours forth the lovely ghee with his bay steeds—may our songs enter you, whose form is golden-bay.
For they have sung together toward the golden womb, urging on the two bay steeds as if to the celestial seat.
To him whom they satisfy with bay steeds as cows do [with milk]—sing a song of power for Indra, who is accompanied by his bay steeds!
That thunderbolt of his is golden, made of iron, golden, and eager; it is golden in his two hands.
Splendid, with beautiful jaws, with golden wrath as its missile—in Indra, the golden forms have been mingled.
Like a banner in heaven, the beloved thunderbolt has been set aloft; it has spread out, golden-hued and swift as a man.
The iron one with golden jaws struck down the dragon; bearing the golden [thunderbolt], he became possessed of a thousand flames.
Time and again, O Indra, you were pleased when praised by the ancient sacrificers with golden hair.
You desire it; all that is worthy of praise belongs to you, O you who are born of bay steeds, your perfect and desirable bounty.

Let the two beloved bay steeds carry Indra—the wielder of the thunderbolt, the exhilarated one, worthy of praise—to the intoxicating draught in his chariot. For him, for Indra, the many libations are desired; the golden Soma juices have flowed forth.
The bay steeds have flowed swiftly for the sake of desire; the bay steeds have urged on the two swift bay horses for the steadfast one.

He who goes according to his pleasure with his bay coursers has attained his desire for the bay ones. The iron-strong one, tawny-bearded and tawny-haired, grew strong at the swift draught, he who is the drinker of the bay juice.
He who, rich in prize-winning steeds, with his bay horses, shall carry us across all difficulties—O Indra, [protect] the two bay steeds!
Whose two golden jaws fly apart like two ladles as he shakes them for the sake of the prize;
when, having drunk of the exhilarating, life-giving food, he cleansed the two bay steeds over the prepared chalice.
And indeed, like a horse to the prize, the Lord of Bay Steeds has neighed at the dwelling of the two beloved ones.
For even the great *dhiṣaṇā* (the sacrificial vessel or inspiration) has been pleased by his might; you, the beloved one, have established great vital strength.
Pervading heaven and earth with your greatness, you, the beloved one, accept our ever-new hymn of praise as something dear.
O Asura, reveal the beloved dwelling of the cow to the golden-hued Sūrya.
O Indra, let the impulses of men bring you, the one who desires them and has golden jaws, upon your chariot.
Drink of the offered mead as you please, delighting in the sacrifice at the joint feast where the ten fingers serve.
O Lord of the Bay Steeds, you have drunk the pressed juices of the ancestors; now this libation is yours alone.
O Indra, the Bull, exhilarate yourself with the honeyed Soma; pour it all at once into your belly.
Those herbs which were born first, three ages before the gods—
I have now reached the hundred and seven abodes of the tawny ones.
O mothers, there are a hundred of your abodes and a thousand of your growths;
therefore, you who possess a hundred powers, make this one of mine free from disease.
Rejoice in the plants, you who bear flowers and produce fruit; like mares that win the prize, may these healing herbs carry us across to safety.
O divine Mothers, the plants—I address this to you.
May I win horses, cattle, and clothing, and your very self, O man. The holy fig tree (*aśvattha*) is your dwelling place; the leaf (*parṇa*) is your abode made for you.
You shall indeed be sharers of cattle, if you win back the man.
Where the plants have gathered together like kings in an assembly, there the inspired sage is called a physician, a slayer of demons and a driver away of disease.
[Bring] the plant rich in horses, rich in Soma, full of vigor, and endowed with great strength.
All the plants have recognized him for his safety.
The plants raise their strength like cows from the stall, they who are about to win wealth; O man, they protect thy very self.
Healing is your mother’s name, and you yourselves are healers.
You are furrows that flow with water; whatever is diseased, you heal it away.
They have stepped over all obstacles like a thief entering a pen.
The plants have driven away whatever malady was in my body.
When I, seeking strength, take these plants in my hand,
the self of disease perishes, as if before one who seizes the living.
O plants, you who creep limb by limb and joint by joint— drive away from there the consumption, like a fierce arbiter.
O consumption, fly away together with the blue jay and the kingfisher!
Perish together with the rush of the wind, perish along with the whirlwind!
Let one of you aid another; let each of you assist her neighbor.
May you all, being in full accord, favor this speech of mine.
Those plants that bear fruit and those that are fruitless, those that blossom and those that are flowerless—
impelled by Bṛhaspati, may they release us from distress.
May they release me from the curse, and likewise from the bond of Varuṇa.
And from the fetter of Yama, and from every sin against the gods—
As they flew down from heaven, the plants spoke:
"The living man whom we have reached, that person shall not suffer harm."
Of those herbs whose king is Soma, many and of a hundredfold vision— of them you are the most excellent, for the fulfillment of desire and for the well-being of the heart.
Of those herbs whose king is Soma, which are spread abroad over the earth...
Impelled by Bṛhaspati, bestow your power upon her.
May he who digs you not be harmed, nor he for whom I dig you. May our bipeds and quadrupeds all remain free from disease.
Those plants that hear this, and those that have gone far away— let all the creepers come together and bestow their power upon her.
The plants hold a consultation with Soma, the king.
O King, we cause him to cross over whomsoever a Brahmin invokes [us] for.
O herb, you are the most excellent; the trees are your subordinates. May he who seeks to harm us be subject to our subordinates.
O Bṛhaspati, come toward me from the gods, whether you be Mitra, Varuṇa, or Pūṣan;
or whether you be with the Ādityas, the Vasus, or accompanied by the Maruts—come as that Parjanya, the showerer, for Śantanu.
O divine messenger, swift and wise, from you, O Devāpi, the gods have come unto me.
Turn toward me; turn back to me. I place within your mouth a radiant word.

O Bṛhaspati, bestow upon us a radiant word within our mouths—one that is free from disease and full of vigor—by which we two may win rain for Śantanu, [and] by which the honeyed drop from heaven has entered [us].
May the honeyed drops enter us; O Indra, bestow upon us a thousand chariots.
Sit down to the office of the Hotar-priest and sacrifice at the proper seasons; O Devāpi, serve the gods with the oblation.
The seer Devāpi, son of Ṛṣṭiṣeṇa, sat down to the office of the Hotar-priest, being wise in the favor of the gods.
He released the celestial waters of rain from the upper ocean down to the lower one.
In that upper ocean, the waters had remained enclosed by the gods;
they flowed forth when released by the son of Ṛṣṭiṣeṇa, Devāpi, and sent by him among the Ṛkṣiṇīs.
When Devāpi, the domestic priest for Śantanu, having been chosen for the office of *hotṛ*, kindled [thee] with compassion;
then Bṛhaspati, bestowing it, granted him speech that is heard by the gods and wins the rain.
O Agni, thee whom Devāpi, the son of Ṛṣṭiṣeṇa, the mortal man, kindled while burning with fervor.
Rejoiced by all the gods, send forth Parjanya who possesses the rain.
O you who are invoked by many, the ancient seers all approached you with their songs at the sacrifices;
come to our sacrifice, O rider of ruddy horses, bringing thousands of chariots unto us.
RV 10.98.10: These ninety-nine thousand offerings, O Agni, have been placed upon your chariot;
with these, O Hero, increase your many bodies. Being impelled, bestow upon us the rain from heaven.
RV 10.98.11: These ninety thousand, O Agni, present as a portion to the bull Indra.
Knowing the paths that lead to the gods according to the seasons, place Aulāna among the gods in heaven.
O Agni, drive away the adversaries; dispel the difficulties, the maladies, and the demons.
From this vast ocean, from the great heaven, release for us here an abundance of waters.
Whom among us do you, the wise one, desire as a wondrous gift—a broad-striding, bellowing bull to be strengthened?
What gift shall we give him at the breaking forth of his power? He fashioned the Vṛtra-slaying thunderbolt and caused it to swell.
For he indeed goes with flashing lightning to the Sāman; through his lordly power, he has taken his seat upon the wide womb.
Overpowering with his kin, he [overcame] the magic powers of his brother Saptatha without his aid.
He went forth for booty on steeds that traverse difficult paths, seeking to win the light of heaven;
unassailable, he seized the hundredfold wealth of the Druhyus, striking down the phallus-worshippers by means of his wondrous form.

He, the mighty one, the courser among the waters, hastens toward the cattle in the contests for booty; where the footless ones, joined together, move without chariots, yet with horses from the wooden troughs, bearing ghee as their fuel.
He, the skillful one whose wealth cannot be reviled, having left his home behind, has come to us, free from blame, along with the Rudras.
I think that the pair of Vamra, having come for food, made him weep and robbed him while he was unbarred.
He, the lord of the house, subdued the Dāsa Tuvīrava, the six-eyed and three-headed.
Trita, strengthened by his power, struck down this boar with his foremost inspired song.
Standing erect against the treacherous man, he has hurled his bolt at the one who seeks to deceive.
He, the most heroic of men, well-born from among us, shattered the fortresses in the slaying of the Dasyus.
Like a rain-cloud pouring water upon the pasture, may he find for us a path to our dwelling.
When he settled upon the soma-drop with his bodies, like a hawk with iron claws, he slew the Dasyus.
With his powerful and mighty [helpers], he delivered Śuṣṇa to Kutsa in his wretched state. He led the praised sage; he won Atka for you and the spoils of men.
This one, bestowing gifts with his manly deeds, is a wondrous magician like Varuṇa among the gods.
This youthful guardian of the seasons has been known; he measured out the four-footed Araru.
Through his hymns, Auśija Ṛjiśvan, like a bull, burst open the enclosure of Pipru.
When he had drunk and the song of the sacrificer shone forth, he went toward the citadels and became preeminent in his splendor.
Thus, O great Asura, Vamraka crept with his feet to Indra for the sake of growth.
Moving forward, may he grant us well-being; he has brought us food, vigor, a secure dwelling, and everything.
O Indra, be firm, O Maghavan; one such as you is our enjoyer here. Praised and drinking the pressed juice, be mindful for our prosperity.
May Savitṛ together with the gods protect us; we choose Aditi, the all-encompassing, for our complete well-being.
Bring forth the seasonal portion for the sacrifice; let the pure one roar toward Vāyu for the sake of the offering.
He who has attained the drinking of the milk of the bull—him we choose for universal well-being and for Aditi.
May the divine Savitṛ impel vigor toward us, for the one who acts uprightly, the sacrificer who presses the soma;
so that we may honor the gods with simple devotion—him we choose for universal well-being and for Aditi.
May Indra be well-disposed toward us at all times; may King Soma attend to our welfare.
Just as they have established the bonds of friendship, we choose Aditi for complete well-being.
Indra has strengthened his body with power through the hymn; O Bṛhaspati, you are the furtherer of this life.
Sacrifice is Manu, our providence, for he is our father; we choose Aditi for universal well-being. Now Indra’s divine power is well-fashioned; Agni is the wise sage, the singer in the house.
And sacrifice has become most beautiful in the assembly; we choose Aditi for universal well-being.

We have not committed many evil deeds against you in secret, nor, O Vasus, have we openly provoked the gods. O gods, let none of us take on the form of falsehood; we choose Aditi for our complete well-being.
May Savitar drive away sickness, and may the mountains push it far away.
RV 10.100.8: Where the stone that presses out the honeyed juice is raised aloft, we choose for ourselves Aditi and universal well-being.
RV 10.100.9: O Vasus, let the pressing-stone stand upright for the presser; drive all enmities far away.
May that god Savitṛ be our praiseworthy protector; we choose for ourselves Aditi and universal well-being.
O cows, eat strength and fatness upon the pasture, you who are anointed at the reservoir in the seat of Cosmic Order (*ṛta*).
Let your very bodies be the medicine for our bodies; we choose Aditi for complete well-being.
The singer is the fulfiller of the will, the protector of all men; Indra indeed is the auspicious providence for those who press the Soma.
We choose for ourselves Aditi’s all-encompassing protection, she whose divine breast is full and from whom we draw our nourishment.
Wondrous is your radiance; your aid fulfills our purpose. There are rivals who seek to overcome us, yet they remain unassailable, for you are the one who bestows long life.
The worshiper, desiring to cross over the boundary, strives toward the cattle and the kine by the straightest path.
Awake, O friends, with one mind; kindle Agni together, you who are many and dwell in the same nest.
I call upon you for protection—Dadhikrā, Agni, and the goddess Uṣas—along with Indra.
Make yourselves joyful; stretch forth your prayers; fashion a ship that carries us across with its oars.
Prepare the weapons; make them ready. Lead the sacrifice forward, O friends.
Yoke the plows; stretch out the yokes. Sow the seed here in the prepared furrow. May our song and our prompt obedience be fruitful. May the sickle come closer to the ripened grain.
The seers yoke the ploughs; they stretch out the yokes separately, the wise ones, desiring favor among the gods. Prepare the water-skins; put on the straps.
Let us pour out the water-bearing well, well-filled, easy to draw from, and inexhaustible.
I pour out the water-bearing well, with its opening cleared, well-roofed, easy to draw from, and inexhaustible.
Satisfy the horses; may you be victorious for our welfare. Prepare the chariot that brings well-being.
Pour out the drink for the heroes into the trough that has wooden buckets, stone wheels, and an iron vessel.
Make a pen, for it is yours, O heroes; sew together armor that is thick and wide.

Make iron fortresses before you, unassailable; let not your cup leak, but hold it firm. O Gods, turn hither your divine, worshipful, and sacrificial wisdom for our protection. May that great Cow, like one who has gone to pasture, yield for us a thousand streams of milk.
Pour forth the golden one into the lap of the wood; fashion him with stone-made axes.
Embrace him with the ten girth-bands; bind the steed to both poles.
The steed, firmly grasping both poles, moves within as if in a womb, his two wives between his legs.
Establish the Lord of the Forest in the wood; set him down, for you have dug out the fountain.
O men, bring forth the prize-winning steed; urge him on, let him leap for the winning of the spoil.
O Niṣṭigrya, send forth your son; with pressing force, bring Indra here to drink the Soma.

May Indra boldly protect your overturned chariot in this glorious battle, O much-invoked one; protect us in the contests for wealth. The wind blew her garment upward when she won a thousand [cows] atop the chariot.
Mudgalānī became the charioteer in the search for cattle; Indra’s army plundered the prize in the battle.
O Indra, ward off the thunderbolt of the one who seeks to strike us, of the one who assails us.
O Maghavan, drive away the weapon of the Dāsa or the Ārya to a distance.
Exulting, he drank from the lake of water; he shattered the peak and advanced against the adversary.
Bearing his testicles as a burden, seeking glory, he stretched out his swift arms, desiring to win.
Approaching him, they made the bull roar and urinate in the midst of the battle.
By him Mudgala won in the contest a well-bred horse, along with a hundred and a thousand cattle. For Kakarda, the bull was yoked; his long-maned charioteer shouted aloud.
As the bull-drawn chariot sped along with its pole, the wife of Mudgala reached out to touch the footprints of the running beast.
And the wise one, knowing [the way], loosened its felloe and yoked the bull there, providing for it;
Indra aided the lord of the cows, and the humped bull hastened along with his feet.
The shaven-headed man moved happily toward the hide-thongs, being bound with wood in the leather strap.
Performing manly deeds for the sake of many people, he seized the cattle and displayed his prowess.
Behold this yoke-mate of the bull, the mallet lying in the midst of the race-course,
by which Mudgala won hundreds and thousands of cattle in the contests for booty.
Far off is evil! Who indeed has seen here that which they yoke and then cause to stand still?
To him they bring neither grass nor water; he bears the burden beyond the yoke-pole, pointing the way.
Like a woman cast aside who finds her husband, she swells like one pouring from a leather bucket.
With this very chariot may we conquer; may our gain be auspicious and full of wealth.
O Indra, you are the eye of the entire moving world, the eye of the eye itself.
When, as a bull, you seek to win the race with your bull-like companion, you urge on even the impotent one as your ally.
Swift, sharpening his weapons like a terrifying bull, the striker, the agitator of the peoples;
Indra, the roaring one, the unblinking, the sole hero, conquered a hundred armies at once. With him who roars, the unblinking, the victorious, the one who stirs up battle, the immovable, the bold.
With Indra, conquer! With him prevail in battle, O men, with the bull who holds arrows in his hand.
He, the controller, is the one who brings together the hosts with those who hold arrows in their hands and those who carry quivers; he is Indra in combat.
He is the victor over those who have joined in fray, the drinker of Soma, strong of arm, wielding a fierce bow, and a shooter with unimpeded arrows.

O Bṛhaspati, fly around with your chariot, slayer of demons, driving away our enemies; shattering the armies, crushing them in battle, and conquering, be the protector of our chariots. Known for his strength, steadfast, a preeminent hero, powerful, vigorous, victorious, and fierce.
O hero, conqueror of men, born of power, O Indra, winner of cattle, mount your victorious chariot!

O kinsmen, follow this one who shatters the cow-stalls, who finds the cattle, whose arm wields the thunderbolt, who conquers the battlefield and crushes the enemy with his might! O friends, be valiant after Indra; hold fast to him!
Plunging with force into the cow-pens, the irresistible hero Indra, of a hundredfold wrath, Irresistible, subduer of armies, and invincible—may he protect our hosts in the battles.
May Indra be their leader; may Bṛhaspati, the sacrificial fee, the sacrifice, and Soma go before them.
Let the Maruts go at the head of the divine armies that shatter and conquer.
Let the fierce host of the Ādityas, of King Varuṇa, and of Indra the Bull go forth.
The shout of the high-minded, world-shaking gods has arisen as they triumph.
O Maghavan, rouse up our weapons; rouse up the spirits of my warriors.
O slayer of Vṛtra, rouse up the vigor of the steeds; let the shouts of the conquering chariots go forth.
May Indra be on our side when the banners meet; may those arrows which are ours be victorious.
May our heroes be superior; O gods, protect us in the battles!
Bewildering their minds, seize their limbs, O *Apvā*; depart to the far distance! Advance against them, burn them up with sorrows in their hearts; let the enemies be overtaken by blinding darkness.
Advance, O heroes, and conquer! May Indra grant you protection. Let your arms be mighty so that you may be invincible.
O Much-invoked One, Soma has been pressed for you; come quickly to the sacrifice with your two bay horses.
To you these songs, brought by inspired heroes, have flowed forth; O Indra, drink of the pressed juice!
O Lord of the Bay Steeds, drink here of that which is shaken in the waters, pressed by the men; fill your belly with it!
O Indra, the stones have yielded this for you; grow strong with them, you who are exhilarated by the hymns and carry them as your vehicle.
I offer a true, forward-flowing draught for the bull’s drinking; O Lord of the Bay Horses, I present this pressed juice to you for your journey.
O Indra, rejoice here with our songs of praise, being lauded by all our prayers and with all our power.
Through your aid, O Lord of Power, and through your heroic might, the seekers who know the Eternal Order (Ṛta) assume vital strength.

O Indra, in the house of man they have stood with offspring, praising you as those who share in the feast. O Lord of the bay horses, through your leadings, the people of the far-reaching, most gracious one offer hymns of praise. O Indra, the singers, receiving your most bountiful aid, have spread themselves abroad through your favors.
O Lord of the Bay Steeds, come with your two Bays to these sacred prayers for the drinking of the pressed soma.
O Indra, the sacrifice has reached you who are attentive; you are the herald of the donor’s rite.
[We call] the Maghavan, the winner of a thousand spoils, the overcomer of enemies, the one who delights in the pressed juice and the well-fashioned hymn.
They attend upon him with songs; they honor Indra, the peerless one, and praise the singer.
The seven divine waters, delightful and inviolable, by which you, O Indra, destroyer of forts, crossed the Sindhu— You found for the gods and for man a path through the ninety-nine flowing streams.
You released the great waters from the curse; you alone, O God, were awake among those who did not wake.
O Indra, with those powers which you exercised in the conquest of Vṛtra, may you nourish your body for all time.
Indra is the heroic will, the one worthy of fair praise; even the voice of song seeks the one invoked by many.
He struck down Vṛtra and made room; Śakra, the helper, has conquered the hostile armies.
We invoke for our welfare the bountiful Indra...
When, O Vasu, will you take pleasure in our hymn? The waters were obstructed at the boundary.
The long-pressed [Soma] for Vātāpya;
whose two bay steeds, well-yoked and moving in different directions, follow the swift ones like two maned stallions, he is the lord of the house.
Indra drove away the evil-born waters like a mortal who, weary and afraid, has grown exhausted;
when the Mighty One harnessed them for glory.
Indra, together with these two, has performed his work, honoring them as they flow along in succession.
Indra is the hero of the two rivers that flow in different directions;
he who stands upon the two maned ones, as wide-spreading as for nourishment—
he, the possessor of beautiful jaws, wins with his two jaws.
He of lofty power has praised; with the lofty ones, the hero has fashioned [his weapons] by his might, like R̥bhu through his insights, like Mātariśvan.
He who, golden-haired and radiant, forged the thunderbolt for the easy slaying of the Dasyu.
With unbroken jaw, you are wondrous and beyond the dust of the world.
Sharpen away our crookedness with your hymn; may we, through the *ṛc*, overcome those who lack the *ṛc*.
Without prayer, the sacrifice does not succeed; it finds favor in you alone.
When your threefold flame rose upward at the yoke-poles of the sacrifice in its dwelling, you were joined with the ship that is self-glorious and brings companionship.
For your glory, the speckled cow became the pouring vessel; for your glory, the flawless ladle was prepared.
With which [power] you pour [the soma] into your own vessel;
when, O Asurya, Sumitra thus praised you a hundred times, Durmitra likewise praised you.
When you aided the son of Kutsa in the slaying of the Dasyus, you protected the child of Kutsa in the slaying of the Dasyus.
Both of you now surely strive for that same goal; you spread out your thoughts like two weavers at their work.
Moving in unison to travel together, you have awakened them; you bestow nourishment like fair days.
Like two oxen at the ploughing-furrows, you take your stand; like two vigorous draft-horses, you exert yourselves for the sake of the divine power.
For you stand like a messenger among men with glory; do not stay away, like two buffalo from the drinking place.

Like the two wings of a bird joined together, like two beautiful beasts, you have come to the sacrificial formula. Like the fire of the god-loving, you shine brightly; like those who travel all around, you sacrifice in many places.
May you be our kinsmen, like a son to his father; like two fierce ones with your splendor, like two lords of men for victory;
like two leaders for prosperity, like two rays for enjoyment—come quickly to our call like those who are prompt to hear!
Like two vigorous stallions on a ridge, like Mitra and Varuṇa, the supporters of Truth, who grant a hundredfold wealth and protection.
In the battle-cry, exalted by vigor, dwelling in the heated chamber, like two rams, they are worthy of worship, full of moisture.
Like two sickles, they are grasping and piercing; like two hunters, they are piercing and rending.
Like two water-born, they are victorious and exhilarating; as such, may they grant me old age that is free from decay and free from death.
Like two *pajrā* birds moving toward their lover, you two, O fierce ones, have overcome obstacles for our sake like two *kṣadmā*.
Like the *Ṛbhus*, you possess swift paths; like Vāyu, you scatter [the clouds], bestowing wealth.
Like the *gharma* vessel, you two are full of sweetness within your bellies; seeking fortune, you two have shattered the enclosure.
Like two birds flying with shimmering luster, you have gone to the desire-stirring, peerless [sacrifice];
like two great ones finding a firm foundation in the depths, like two feet, you have found a footing for one who crosses over.
Like two ears, remember the instruction; like two portions of light, bestow upon us wondrous wealth.
Like two *āraṅgara* birds you hasten toward the honey; like two bees, you descend upon the cow.
